A presidente da Casa, Ivana Bastos (PSD), ressaltou a produtividade da sessão e informou que algumas votações foram antecipadas devido à Marcha dos Prefeitos, que impactará a presença dos deputados na ALBA entre 18 e 21 de maio.

text:
Microplastics in your daily drinks — by the numbers

❗️Tap water: up to 5.5 particles per liter.
❗️Milk in carton packaging: up to 11.
❗️Juice in plastic packaging: up to 41.
❗️Hot coffee in a paper cup: up to 250,000.

Yes — paper cups. The interior is lined with a thin polyethylene film to make it waterproof. When hot liquid (above 85°C) sits against that lining, the plastic begins to shed micro- and nanoparticles directly into your drink. 

A 2022 study found that a single 12-oz paper cup can release tens of thousands of microplastic particles within 15 minutes of contact with hot liquid.

From a TCM perspective, these are subtle, accumulating toxins - what we’d consider a slow burden on the Liver (detoxification), the Spleen (the gut barrier and microbiome), and over time, the Kidney essence (Jing) through endocrine disruption.

What helps:
👉🏻 A glass or stainless steel travel mug for hot drinks
👉🏻 Filtered water (carbon block + reverse osmosis where possible)
👉🏻 Glass-bottled milk and juice where available
👉🏻 Daily support for elimination: fiber, hydration, sweating, regular bowel movements
👉🏻 Bitter greens, cruciferous vegetables, and herbs that support Liver phase II detox

We can’t fully escape microplastics. But we can drastically reduce daily exposure - and we can support the body’s clearance pathways

“OH, you’re so yeet hay (熱氣)!” 

One of the most common phrases about your body condition I’ve grown up with in a Cantonese household. 熱氣 literally means “hot air” — but in TCM it’s a real thing. it means your body has built up too much internal heat, and it’s showing up EVERYWHERE.

There are 2 simple ways to look at from a TCM perspective:

🔴 EXCESS HEAT (the loud one): you feel it fast and strong and often associated with eating fried or spicy foods, overly heaty conditions, or lack of sleep. The heating system in your body has gone crazy.

Siihen mahtui odotusta, surua, toivoa, luopumista ja paljon hiljaisia hetkiä, jolloin elämä opetti kärsivällisyyttä tavalla, jota en olisi koskaan itse valinnut. Kiinalaisessa lääketieteessä sydäntä pidetään ihmisen hengen, Shenin, kotina. Sydän kantaa rakkautta, iloa, yhteyttä ja kykyä olla läsnä toiselle ihmiselle. Äitiys onkin paljon enemmän kuin kehon prosessi — se on sydämen avautumista, hoivaa, turvaa ja elämän kannattelemista.

Kiinalaisen lääketieteen mukaan myös pitkät odotuksen ja epävarmuuden ajat vaikuttavat ihmiseen syvästi. Huoli sitoo energiaa, suru kuluttaa ja jatkuva ikävä voi väsyttää koko kehoa ja mieltä. Mutta samalla ajatellaan, että vaikeudet voivat kasvattaa sydämen syvyyttä ja myötätuntoa. Tänään ymmärrän sen.

Matkani äidiksi adoption kautta opetti minulle luottamusta elämään. Opin, ettei kaikkea voi kontrolloida eikä suurimpia lahjoja voi aina saada silloin tai sillä tavalla kuin itse toivoo. Joskus elämä johdattaa meidät täysin toista polkua pitkin — ja vasta myöhemmin ymmärrämme, miksi.

Tänään äitienpäivänä tunnen kiitollisuutta siitä, että sain kulkea juuri tämän matkan. Vaikka siihen liittyi myös kipua, se teki minusta ihmisen, joka osaa pysähtyä rakkauden äärelle aivan eri tavalla.

Kiinalaisessa lääketieteessä ajatellaan, että kun sydän on avoin ja elämä saa virrata omassa rytmissään, asiat löytävät lopulta oikean paikkansa. Ehkä juuri siksi kaikkein suurimmat lahjat saapuvat usein elämäämme reittiä, jota emme olisi koskaan itse osanneet kuvitella.

Naisen keho muistaa rakkauden, surun ja hoivan sukupolvien yli

Äitienpäivänä huomioni kiinnittyy siihen, miten paljon naisissa kulkee mukana sellaista, mitä ei voi nähdä ulospäin.
Sukupolvelta toiselle siirtyvät eleet, tavat, hiljaiset roolit ja kyky pitää elämästä kiinni vaikeinakin hetkinä.

Moni nainen on oppinut jo varhain tunnistamaan muiden tarpeet ennen omiaan. Olemaan se, joka kannattelee arkea, huolehtii, joustaa ja rakastaa silloinkin, kun oma keho väsyy. Usein tätä ei opeteta sanoilla, vaan se siirtyy eteenpäin katseissa, kosketuksessa ja siinä tavassa, jolla ympärillä olevat naiset ovat kohdanneet maailman.

Kiinalaisessa lääketieteessä ajatellaan, ettei keho erottele fyysistä ja emotionaalista kokemusta toisistaan. Pitkä suru, jatkuva vastuunkanto ja elämän kuormitus voivat jäädä kehoon hiljaisena valppautena. Mutta keho kantaa mukanaan myös jotain muuta — rakkautta, lempeyttä, lohtua ja kykyä nähdä hyvää silloinkin, kun elämä ei ole ollut helppoa.

Vastaanotolla tämän huomaa usein pienistä hetkistä. Siitä, kuinka keho pehmenee, kun ihminen kokee tulevansa nähdyksi ilman vaatimuksia. Kuinka hengitys syvenee, kun mitään ei tarvitse hetkeen kantaa yksin.

Ehkä juuri siksi hoidon tärkein tehtävä ei aina ole korjata rikki mennyttä. Joskus tärkeintä on muistuttaa kehoa siitä, että sen ei tarvitse olla jatkuvasti vahva.

Ajattelen, että yksi kauneimmista asioista, joita voimme siirtää eteenpäin seuraaville sukupolville, on kyky rakastaa lempeästi — myös itseämme. Kyky levätä ilman syyllisyyttä. Kyky nähdä maailmassa hyvää kaiken keskellä.

Hyvää äitienpäivää 🤍

Toivon tähän päivään iloa, rakkautta, pehmeyttä ja hetkiä, joissa tunnet olevasi kannateltu.

Before you scroll…go take a look at your tongue in the mirror.

Tongue mapping is rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine and has been used for centuries as a non-invasive way to assess what’s happening inside the body. Practitioners view the tongue as a reflection of digestion, circulation, hydration, and overall internal balance.

This is one of my favorite ways, alongside bloodwork, for spotting patterns, dysfunction, and disease.

Here are a few common things to look for:
👉 Light pink tongue: generally a sign of balance and healthy circulation
👉 Bright red tongue: can point to heat or inflammation in the body
👉 Pale or white tongue: indicates low energy, poor circulation, or possible deficiencies
👉 Thick white coating: often tied to digestive imbalance or gut issues
👉 Yellow coating: points to heat and inflammation deeper in the gut
👉 Purple or bluish tint: indicates poor circulation or stagnation in the body
👉 Ridges or scalloped edges: associated with nutrient deficiencies or stress on the system

This is why I love combining tools like this with functional bloodwork…because while your tongue can give you clues, bloodwork helps you go deeper and actually understand what’s happening beneath the surface.

So when would I personally give paracetamol to my child?

Usually:
• If it is nighttime (because sometimes I may fall asleep too, and I worry that I may not be able to monitor my child closely)
• Fever is above 38.5°C
• My child is uncomfortable and having difficulty falling asleep

…I may choose to give paracetamol to help reduce the fever and allow my child to rest more comfortably.

I also want to clarify something that many parents may misunderstand:

A lot of people think:
“Paracetamol can reduce fever quickly, but TCM medicine cannot.”

But actually, suitable TCM medicine can also reduce fever quite fast.

The key difference is:
In TCM, the medicine must MATCH the syndrome pattern.

So if a TCM fever-relief medicine does not seem effective, sometimes it is not because “TCM doesn’t work” — it may simply mean that the medicine is not suitable for that particular syndrome pattern.

Of course, general fever-relief TCM medicine may still help in some situations, but proper syndrome differentiation is still very important.

Hopefully this gives parents another perspective on managing children’s fever ❤️

Fever is extremely common in early childhood, and sometimes what children need most is:
✔️ proper assessment
✔️ close monitoring
✔️ hydration
✔️ rest
✔️ and calm parents 😊

⚠️ Seek immediate medical attention if your child develops:
• breathing difficulty
• persistent lethargy
• seizures
• dehydration
• persistent high fever
• poor responsiveness
• or if you are worried about your child’s condition

If you have any general questions about children’s fever, TCM management, pediatric tuina, feel free to leave them in the comment box below 😊

post_owner.name: Physician Wong Ying Xin
text:
As a TCM physician and also a mummy, one of the questions I get very often is:

“When should I give my child paracetamol when they have fever?”

So today, I thought I’d share how I personally manage my own child’s fever from a TCM physician perspective.

When my child develops a fever, the first thing I do is:
✔️ Measure the body temperature
✔️ Observe the tongue
✔️ Check the pulse / look at the capillary vessel on the index finger

Based on the symptoms and signs, I will first make a diagnosis.

This is also why, for parents, I usually advise:
Please let medical professionals assess the child properly, because there are many different reasons why children develop fever.

If the condition is suitable for TCM treatment, I may prescribe TCM medicine and do pediatric tuina such as 清天河水 to help relieve the fever.

Personally, I usually prefer to give TCM medicine in the daytime because it is easier for me to monitor my child’s condition closely.

Very often, if the medicine is suitable, the fever may start to subside within about 2 hours. My child may begin sweating and gradually fall asleep.

In general, if:
✔️ the child is still relatively active (maybe slightly whiny, which is understandable 😅)
✔️ and the temperature is still below around 38.5–39°C

…I will usually continue monitoring first.

During fever episodes, appetite often decreases — and that is okay. The important things are:
• hydration
• sponging
• adequate rest

Sometimes, even if the fever is 39°C and above, I may still choose to continue with TCM medicine — but ONLY because I am very clear about what is happening with my child’s condition.

For parents, if you are unsure, you may consider giving paracetamol when the temperature is above 38.5°C, following the doctor’s advice.

⚠️ Very important:
Paracetamol dosage must be according to the child’s WEIGHT, not just age.

If unsure, please call the clinic or medical centre that prescribed the medicine to confirm the dosage.

• Pomaga odciążyć kręgosłup.

One thing I did throughout my bodybuilding “career” is chase scale weight show after show. 

Always thinking that because I looked a certain way at X weight that to match that look or improve on my previous look I needed to be X weight again. 

Knowing what I know now I would slap myself repeatedly until I understood the assignment…..it’s in the name bodyBUILDING. 

There is no doubt that you can improve your previous look and come in around the same weight (better condition, drier and even fuller), but to make proper progression we have to step outside our comfort zone and in my case that’s the number I THINK the scales represents.

To many people in prep allow the scales dictate every decision. All logic goes out the window. 

The goal isn’t to become lighter every single week.The goal is to build a better physique.

And sometimes becoming a better bodybuilder means accepting that the scale has to go UP in the off-season to create enough tissue to actually look different on stage.

You cannot expect a radically improved physique while being afraid of bodyweight increases.

At some point you have to stop chasing a number and start chasing development.

👉 Zupa z czerwonej soczewicy jest bogata w białko roślinne i błonnik, dzięki czemu daje uczucie sytości na długo i pomaga ograniczyć podjadanie między posiłkami. To sprawia, że świetnie sprawdza się u osób, które chcą zdrowiej jeść albo kontrolować masę ciała. Czerwona soczewica dobrze wpływa również na układ trawienny.

👉 Zawarty w niej błonnik wspiera pracę jelit, poprawia trawienie i pomaga utrzymać prawidłową florę bakteryjną.

👉 Poznaj przepis na delikatną zupę wspierającą jelita i spokojne trawienie:
1. Do dużego garnka wlewamy 3 litry wody lub lekkiego rosołu i zagotowujemy.
2. Na maśle klarowanym delikatnie dusimy 1 cebulkę, 2 nieduże marcheweczki oraz 1 pietruszkę pokrojone w drobną kostkę. Warzywa mają być miękkie, lekko słodkie i spokojnie podduszone, nie przypalone.
3. Podduszone warzywa przekładamy do garnka.
4. Dodajemy 1 ziemniaka pokrojonego w kostkę.
5. Następnie dodajemy 2 szklanki czerwonej soczewicy, która była moczona 24 godziny w zimnej wodzie, później odcedzona i ponownie zalana gorącą wodą na kolejne 24 godziny.
6. Tak przygotowana soczewica jest łagodniejsza dla przewodu pokarmowego i lepiej tolerowana przez jelita.
7. Całość gotujemy około 40 minut na bardzo małym ogniu.
8. Zupa powinna być ciepła, delikatna i dobrze ugotowana.
9. Można podać ją z odrobiną masła klarowanego lub świeżymi ziołami.

👉 Dlaczego moczymy soczewicę?
• Moczenie zmniejsza ilość substancji antyodżywczych obecnych naturalnie w roślinach strączkowych.
• Pomaga ograniczyć fermentację i wzdęcia.
• Poprawia strawność i tolerancję jelitową.
• Zmniejsza obciążenie przewodu pokarmowego.
• Dobrze przygotowana soczewica jest spokojniejsza dla mikrobioty i układu trawiennego.

👉 To właśnie takich prostych zasad uczymy w programie Polskie Zdrowie. Pokażemy Ci jak gotować tak, żeby jedzenie naprawdę wspierało jelita, energię i codzienne funkcjonowanie. Wpisuj w komentarzu POLSKA, a otrzymasz zaproszenie do programu.

Dein Bauch denkt mit.
Und oft kennt er die Antwort, bevor dein Kopf sie findet.

Du kennst das:

Du sagst noch „Ja“ — und spürst es schon im Bauch.
Ein Ziehen. Ein Engerwerden.

Der Bauch hat die Entscheidung längst gespürt.

In deinem Verdauungstrakt liegen rund 100 Millionen Nervenzellen — mehr als im Rückenmark.

Was kannst du gerade nicht verdauen?

Do you feel bloated all the time? 

In Chinese Medicine, bloating isn’t just a simple digestive issue. It can come from two completely different root causes.
 
The first is Spleen Qi deficiency.
 
Your spleen is responsible for turning food into energy. 
 
When its energy is weak, digestion slows down and food isn’t processed efficiently, leading to fullness and bloating. 
 
This type of bloating usually gets worse when you’re tired and especially after eating, particularly raw or cold foods like salads.

The second type is Liver Qi stagnation.
 
This is more related to stress and emotional tension. 
 
Your liver controls the smooth flow of energy in your body, including digestion. 
 
When that flow gets stuck due to stress, pressure, or late nights, it can disrupt your stomach and spleen. 
 
This type of bloating is often felt more in the lower abdomen, gets worse around your period, and doesn’t feel better even after using the bathroom.
 
So two people can both feel bloated but one needs to strengthen digestion, while the other needs to improve energy flow in the body.

Veel vrouwen lopen rond met klachten…
zonder te weten dat hun Nierfunctiekring hierin een grote rol speelt.

Lage rugpijn, oorsuizen, weinig libido, vaak moeten plassen of een verzwakt gebit, het zijn signalen die je lichaam je geeft…
maar die vaak worden genegeerd.

Binnen de Chinese geneeskunde worden de Nieren gezien als de basis van je energie.

Je basis.

maar ook van binnen.

Onrust.
Een gevoel van spanning.

acupressuur is geen losse oplossing, maar een onderdeel van een bredere aanpak.

text:
I was giving the keynote talk on perimenopause at the <redacted_mention> conference on Thursday, and someone asked what the SINGLE most essential thing is for a woman going through perimenopause that applies to all women. Of course, years ago, I would have said something like nutrition since I studied nutrition science all my life, but I had to pause...

My answer was to be in alignment with circadian rhythms. We can’t change time. Time changes us. When we try to go against the confines of time, we see health issues. Ancient traditions such as Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine embodied these concepts well before the development of circadian rhythm science.

We are run by the Sun. In addition, we need to honor the cycles of the Moon and embrace the night. Within this framework, we then set the stage for eating, sleeping, relaxing, moving, thinking, doing, and being.

Everything starts and ends with time. ⏰🪐

In Chinese medicine, it has been used as a precious tonic, especially when the body is dry, weak, depleted, or recovering.

Modern research has found compounds such as proteins, glycoproteins, amino acids, minerals, and sialic acid.
Some studies also discuss EGF-like activity, which may be connected with skin repair, hydration, and tissue support.

It is not a cure-all.
And it is not automatically good for everyone.

👉 Piołun ogrodowy to jedno z najstarszych ziół stosowanych w medycynie naturalnej.

👉 Ma intensywnie gorzki smak, który nie jest przypadkowy. To właśnie gorycz odpowiada za jego działanie regulujące metabolizm.

👉 Piołun pobudza wydzielanie żółci, wspiera trawienie, odciąża wątrobę i pomaga przy uczuciu ciężkości po jedzeniu.

👉 Zawiera substancje aktywne takie jak gorycze roślinne, olejki eteryczne, flawonoidy i związki wspierające pracę układu pokarmowego.

👉 W medycynie chińskiej smak gorzki należy do elementu Ognia. Wzmacnia serce i jednocześnie rozprasza zastój w wątrobie. Dodatkowo wspiera element Ziemi, czyli śledzionę i trawienie.

👉 Dlatego działa jednocześnie na emocje, metabolizm i układ pokarmowy. Tradycyjnie piołun stosowano w nalewkach trawiennych. Dzisiaj można go używać w prostszej formie, jako napar.

👉 5 dobrych rad:
1. Pij napar z piołunu przy uczuciu ciężkości, wzdęciach i spowolnionym trawieniu.
2. Stosuj krótkimi cyklami, nie codziennie przez długi czas.
3. Najlepiej pić małe ilości, około pół szklanki naparu.
4. Unikaj stosowania na czczo przy wrażliwym żołądku.
5. Nie stosuj w ciąży i przy silnych dolegliwościach bez konsultacji.

👉 Piołun to proste narzędzie, które możesz wprowadzić w codzienność, jeżeli chcesz wesprzeć wątrobę i trawienie.

👉 Jeżeli chcesz zrobić to głębiej, systemowo i świadomie, zapraszam Cię do dalszej pracy. Prowadzę program Polskie Zdrowie, w którym uczymy się pracy z metabolizmem, wątrobą i całym organizmem krok po kroku.

This comes up a lot.

People feel better on carnivore and assume meat must be the answer.

And yes, in the short term, that can absolutely happen.

When you remove gluten, processed foods, and a lot of common irritants, inflammation often goes down. But that does not mean the root issue has been resolved.

You can quiet symptoms by removing triggers, or you can work to restore the system so it can tolerate and thrive on a broader range of foods.

Die allerbesten Proteine und Nahrungsergänzungsmittel bringen nichts, wenn der Körper nicht in der Lage ist, diese aufzunehmen. Und das ist ein sehr wichtiger Aspekt, den die TCM berücksichtigt. 

Alles, was wir essen,  muss in der Mitte verstoffwechselt werden. Und dazu braucht es Wärme und Regelmäßigkeit. Ganz einfach, in Form von warmen Essen mit proteinhaltigen Lebensmitteln. 

Wenn kein Fisch oder Fleisch, dann Hülsenfrüchte. Und hier hilft es nicht einmal viel zu essen, sondern viel wichtiger ist es regelmäßig kleine Portionen in die Ernährung zu integrieren. Täglich. 

Und bevor ich mir Sorgen mache, um Grammzahlen, sollte ich prüfen, ob meine Mitte überhaupt gut funktioniert. Nur dann kann sie die Proteine auch gut aufnehmen und ist nicht mit einer übermäßigen Ausscheidung beschäftigt. 

Zeichen, dass die Mitte gut funktioniert: 
- Der Bauch fühlt sich warm und wohlig an
- Kaum Blähungen, keine Schmerzen
- Regelmäßige Verdauung, ohne Beschwerden
- Gute Energie 

Wenn das alles passt, kannst du beginnen, täglich kleine Portionen gekochte Hülsenfrüchte in deine Ernährung zu integrieren. Oder mal Fisch/Fleisch. Je nachdem, wie du dich ernährst.

As a 40 year old Doctor & TCM expert, I look at hormones holistically. And these 4 mistakes are so common in women 30/ 40+

1. Not eating enough protein 
👉🏼 protein is important not just for hair and muscle but to support blood sugar, ovulation, hormone production, and satiety. You should eat at least 1.2-1.6 g/kg body weight protein per day. Very active and perimenopausal women even more. 

2. Fasting too long.
👉🏼 most fasting studies have been done on men. But women’s cycles react more sensitively cortisol which can be increased through fasting. So better windows are 12 to 13 hours overnight, not longer. 

3. Too much HIIT/ wrong timing 
👉🏼 high intensity training can increase cortisol, especially in the 10 to 7 days before your period. Many women tolerate different types of training better. Cortisol chronically raised can further impact skin & hormones. 

4. Coffee on an empty stomach.
👉🏼 not only relevant for your stomach, especially in sensitive women, but for raising cortisol that is already peaking in the morning naturally. Better: breakfast with protein first, then coffee.

text:
strong BONE MILK 💪🏼 aka Black Sesame Milk 🖤 + aids in premature greying hair and strength ✨

〰️ tap the heart, share and follow along 〰️

In TCM (traditional Chinese medicine) black sesame is used to support hair pigment - melanin - strength and healthy ageing 💫

It is amongst the highest sources of CALCIUM needed for healthy bone structure:

Calcium (per 100 ml)
🥛 dairy milk ~120 mg
🖤 black sesame milk ~120–200 mg
💡 must be soaked overnight to reduce phytates - compounds that block mineral absorption, this is the way to bring the nutrition profile closer to dairy milk.

🧠 How to maximise benefits
✨ Vitamin D → helps absorb calcium (sunlight, oily fish, egg yolks, supplement)
✨ Vitamin C → boosts iron absorption (berries, citrus, kiwi and others)
✨ Vitamin K2 → directs calcium to bones (leafy greens, fermented foods, cheese)
✨ Omega 6 → not to fear, naturally occurring, so just balance by including chia, ground flax, walnuts, fish or supplements in your overall diet.

⚠️ Avoid around it:
✨ Coffee & tea → reduce mineral absorption (leave ~1 hour gap)
✨ Too much salt → increases calcium loss

Full recipe below 👇🏼

Black Sesame Milk 🖤🥛
✨ 3/4 cup black sesame (100g)
✨ 2 1/2 – 3 cups cold water (adjust for creaminess / ~650 ml or more)
✨ Pinch of salt
✨ 2 Medjool dates, soaked
or 1/2 – 1 tbsp maple / honey / date syrup
✨ 1 tsp vanilla extract

Soak the dates in hot water, and the sesame seeds overnight in cold water (just enough to fully submerge). While they won’t plump like nuts, soaking helps soften the seeds and reduce phytic acid, improving mineral absorption and texture. The next day, drain and rinse well. Add everything to a blender and blend until smooth, adjusting water to your preferred consistency. Strain through a nut milk bag, or a fine strainer using the back of a spoon. Optional: re-blend the pulp with a little water and strain again to extract more milk.
- Use leftover pulp in oats, yogurt, smoothies, pancake batter or granola
- Store in the fridge and shake well / stir before each use

Food is both science and spirit.

Through the lens of Western science, we see nutrients, biochemistry, and physiology. Through Eastern traditions like Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine, we see energy, flow, and connection. 

When these perspectives meet, a more complete picture of nourishment emerges. Each color, each system, each layer of the body reflects a different conversation between what we eat and how we live, think, and feel. text:
running fire cupping vs stationary cupping — what’s the actual difference? 

both come from the same root in traditional Chinese medicine, but they’re used very differently depending on the goal. 

🔥 running fire cupping (sliding cupping) 
TCM perspective: used to “move qi and blood” across a larger area, release stagnation, and open the channels without strongly localizing the treatment. especially helpful for muscle tension, early-stage colds, or when the body needs movement rather than extraction. 

biomedical perspective: the continuous gliding motion increases local circulation, warms tissue, and may reduce fascial adhesions. it’s often experienced as less intense because suction is dynamic, not fixed — more like a deep tissue massage with decompression. 

🫧 stationary cupping (with or without fire) 
TCM perspective: used to “draw out” stagnation, toxins, heat, or dampness from a specific area. it localizes treatment — great for stubborn pain points, respiratory conditions, or deeper stagnation patterns. 

biomedical perspective: sustained negative pressure increases blood flow to a targeted area, promotes microcirculation, and may trigger an anti-inflammatory response. this is what often leaves the classic circular marks — a sign of localized tissue response, not “damage.” 

✨ key difference: 
running cupping = movement + circulation across tissues 
stationary cupping = targeted decompression + localized response 

both have therapeutic value — the technique depends on what your body actually needs.

Gestern sagte eine Klientin aus meinem Gruppenprogramm zu mir:

„Ich spüre jetzt endlich,
was du die ganze Zeit meinst.“

Nicht verstehen. Spüren.

Dieses eine Wort beschreibt den ganzen Unterschied, um den es in somatischer Arbeit geht.

Sie war seit sechs Wochen dabei.
Auf kognitiver Ebene hatte sie alles schon in Woche eins verstanden:
das Nervensystem, den Vagusnerv, die verschiedenen Zustände.
Sie hätte es dir perfekt erklären können.

Und trotzdem hat sich nichts verändert –
bis ihr Körper nachgezogen hat.

Es passierte während einer Atemübung.
Kein großer Moment.
Nur ein ruhiges Ausatmen…
und plötzlich merkte sie, wie sich ihr Kiefer löste –
ohne dass sie es bewusst gesteuert hat.

Das ist Regulation.
Nichts, was du aktiv „machst“.
Sondern etwas, das dein Körper zulässt, wenn er sich sicher genug fühlt.

Wir verbringen so viel Zeit damit, zu verstehen.
Zu lernen. Zu optimieren.
Und ja – das ist wertvoll.

Aber das ist top-down.

Das Nervensystem arbeitet bottom-up.
Körper zuerst. Der Kopf folgt.

Wenn du also genau weißt, was du tun solltest –
es aber einfach nicht umsetzen kannst,
dann ist das vielleicht kein Disziplinproblem.

Sondern ein Sicherheitsproblem.

Und das verändert alles.

Du möchtest raus aus dem Funktionieren? Dann DM mir „BEREIT“ für einen Platz im Gruppenprogramm ab 20. Mai. Ich schick dir die Infos.

text:
Today is Earth Day and if I can encourage you to do one thing, go outside and smell the flowers.

Being in balance with, and aligning to, nature is fundamental to Taoism. Immersing yourself in the natural world has many benefits, from supporting the immune system to reducing stress hormones and boosting creativity.

So many of us spend the whole day indoors, glued to a screen. Yet stepping away from this and getting outside is about far more than fresh air. 

Your eyes naturally respond well to the shapes and patterns found in nature, which have been shown to relax the nervous system. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Liver is said to open to the eyes, so nourishing the eyes also supports Liver energy.

Simply seeing nature has also been linked with increased positive emotions, which may help encourage healthy anti inflammatory responses in the body. Even a plant on your desk can help.

It’s the smallest acts of self-care that make the biggest difference, nature has am amazing way of bringing us back into balance.

#EarthDay #NatureHealing #ChineseMedicine #TCM #Taoism

This circa 1920 watercolour is a copy of an ancient original and can be found in the @wellcomecollection, along with other visual material featuring the Shen Nong.⁠⠀⁠
⁠⠀⁠
Legend has it that Shen Nong (神农), or ‘Divine Farmer’, was one of the Three Sovereigns, a group of mythological rulers and deities from ancient China circa 2852 to 2070 BC who established the Chinese life-arts. Said to have been born the son of a princess and a heavenly dragon, Shen Nong is believed to have taught the ancient Chinese their practices of agriculture, as well as the use of herbal drugs, which became the foundation of traditional Chinese medicine.⁠⠀⁠
⁠⠀⁠
Tea is allegedly one of his great discoveries, as it proved to be the antidote for almost 70 varieties of poisons. Shen Nong discovered tea by accident when the tea leaves from twigs he was using for a fire rose up on a column of hot air and landed in the water he was trying to boil. Being a keen herbalist, he tasted the resulting brew and this became the origins of tea. Shen Nong tasted hundreds of herbs in order to determine their medicinal value.⁠⠀⁠
⁠⠀⁠
The story of Shen Nong has been passed down orally for centuries and has been differently embellished throughout histories. Some versions even claim Shen Nong had a see-through stomach that allowed him to see the effects of various herbs on his internal organs.⁠⠀⁠
⁠⠀⁠

🔥 Gewürze wie Kardamom, Muskat, Wacholderbeere oder Lorbeer bringen Wärme und Bewegung in deinen Bauch. Genau das braucht dein Stoffwechsel, um richtig zu arbeiten.

Wenn du diese drei Dinge in deinen Alltag integrierst, schaffst du die Grundlage dafür, dass dein Körper Energie bildet und Nährstoffe optimal verwertet.

text:
This is a traditional Chinese sweet soup (drank hot or chilled) that provides:

-skin hydration
-enhances collagen production, skin elasticity 
-nourishes the lungs
-aids in digestion, helps prevent constipation

Snow fungus or white fungus is a very common ingredient for Chinese cuisine and TCM. It’s seen as a beauty tonic and it’s something that I grew up drinking & appreciating its health benefits.

My family likes to add papaya for its vitamin A, C, E, boost immunity, and enzyme content to boost digestion and jujube/red dates— rich in antioxidants, Vitamin C, and fiber. 

To prepare, you have to soak the snow fungus for at least 30 minutes; to soften and remove any hard parts that would be hard to chew like its core. Then, cook until tender. It should have a gelatinous texture. If your snow fungus is dirty, cook until tender then rinse out and add it back to a pot of water to boil.

Then you can add the papaya, jujube, and a bit of rock sugar for taste. 

Leave a comment if you tried this and what do you think?

#snowfungus #tcm #chinesebeauty #skincaretips #snowfungussoup

This comes up a lot - and the answer surprises people every time.
In East Asian Medicine, meridians are not the same as organs. They are energy channels that run throughout the entire body and cannot be surgically removed. They are present until we stop breathing.

When an organ is removed, the channel - the meridian - remains. The organ itself acts like a reservoir for that channel, but the channel continues to flow. And because meridians are bilateral, you have the gallbladder channel running on both sides of your body regardless.

This means if you’ve had your gallbladder out, you can still work with that meridian through qigong, cupping, tracing, and acupressure. The system is still there and still accessible.

As apurações também levantam questionamentos sobre possível direcionamento no certame, o que deve ser analisado pelos órgãos de controle, incluindo o Ministério Público do Estado do Pará.

Stress is the health epidemic of the 21st century and an issue I constantly see in my clinic.

The thing is stress is totally normal, it’s how the body reacts when it feels threatened. In times gone by, after being chased by a tiger, the body would have naturally regulated itself because a period of rest would have rebalanced the body. 

In Chinese Medicine we call this the Yin/Yang axis. During the fight or flight response Yang energy is what will enable the body to act and Yin is the nourishing force that enables the body to recover and heal.

The problem with modern living is that we are so sedentary with constant stress, which means our Yin/Yang axis becomes out of balance. This affects our five key organs, especially our Kidney’s, resulting in stress-related symptoms including poor skin, sluggish digestion and insomnia.

Thankfully, this is surprisingly easy to resolve. So in honour of Stress Awareness Month, I’m sharing a few simple techniques to keep the body in balance and clear accumulated stress.

text:
An herbal probiotic known as Shen Qu, a mix of six grains and herbs that are fermented, cooked, and formed into blocks. It is an herb widely used in Chinese medicine formulas (including Bao He Wan, available on our site) to improve digestion and gut health.

A remarkably effective all-natural digestive enzyme, it’s also the Chinese herb I find the most ingenious, since unlike probiotics, it retains its medicinal benefits for years and without requiring refrigeration!

A medicinal ingredient used since the early 3rd century, Shen Qu (also known as Six Leaven) is comprised of Artemisia annua, Polygonum hydropiper, Xanthium sibiricum, adzuki bean, bitter almond, and wheat bran—fermented together.

Originally invented as a nutrient to grow yeast as a starter for making wine, it became better known as a medicinal for aiding digestion. Shen Qu “acts as a digestive and relies on abundant microbial enzymes and wheat bran fiber, which promotes intestinal peristalsis,” the wave-like muscle contractions that move food through the digestive tract.

Modern clinical studies have shown that Shen Qu has anti-inflammatory and intestinal mucosal barrier repairing effects (Bose et al, 2012). Studies also demonstrate its ability to reduce harmful bacteria colonization (Wang et al, 2018), while significantly increasing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium (Fu et al, 2020), the “good bacteria” found in probiotic supplements.

To relieve food stagnation, Shen Qu is ideally taken with hawthorn (which aids in protein and fat digestion) and a piece of orange peel. Bao He Wan, an herbal formula available on our site, leads with Shen Qu and hawthorn, highlighted in earlier videos for its ability to improve digestion, reduce cholesterol, support heart health, and assist in weight loss—and also contains several other herbs including Chen Pi, or aged orange peel. It’s one of the most-recommended formulas in TCM for better digestion, making it particularly helpful during the holiday season. Bao He Wan is also safe for dogs!

Wanneer mensen klachten ervaren rond de buik, wordt er al snel gedacht aan voeding of beweging als primaire oorzaak. 

In de praktijk zie ik echter dat dit gebied vaak meer vertelt over wat er intern gebeurt, met name op het niveau van spanning en circulatie.

Binnen de Chinese geneeskunde speelt de Dai Mai, de zogenoemde gordelmeridiaan, hierin een centrale rol. Deze meridiaan loopt horizontaal rond het middel en functioneert als een verbindende structuur die de stroming van Qi en Bloed tussen het boven- en onderlichaam coördineert.

Wanneer het lichaam langdurig onder spanning staat, of wanneer emoties onvoldoende worden verwerkt, zie je dat juist deze zone zich sluit. De ademhaling wordt beperkter, de circulatie vertraagt en de samenwerking tussen Lever-, Milt- en Maagfunctiekring raakt verstoord.

Het activeren van de Dai Mai richt zich daarom niet op symptoombestrijding, maar op het herstellen van beweging binnen het systeem. Wanneer de circulatie verbetert, krijgt het lichaam opnieuw de ruimte om los te laten.

text:
O Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios da Bahia (TCM-BA) aplicou multa de R$ 6 mil à ex-prefeita de Lauro de Freitas, Moema Gramacho, após identificar irregularidades em contratos que somam mais de R$ 6,7 milhões.

A decisão tem como base auditoria que analisou a locação e manutenção de aparelhos de ar-condicionado entre 2019 e 2023. O processo envolve o Pregão Presencial nº 026/2018 e o Contrato nº 272/2019, que previam o uso de cerca de 720 equipamentos.

Segundo o relatório técnico, houve problemas já na fase de planejamento. Entre as principais falhas está a ausência de estudos que justificassem a escolha pela locação dos aparelhos, em vez da compra.

Além disso, a pesquisa de preços foi considerada inadequada, por ter sido baseada apenas em cotações de empresas privadas, sem referência a valores públicos.

Durante a execução do contrato, a auditoria apontou falta de controle sobre a manutenção dos equipamentos e irregularidades na instalação. Em visitas técnicas, foram encontrados aparelhos danificados em unidades da administração municipal.

O corpo técnico chegou a estimar um possível prejuízo de R$ 2,7 milhões aos cofres públicos. No entanto, a falta de dados mais precisos impediu a comprovação exata do dano, o que afastou a obrigação de ressarcimento.

O Ministério Público de Contas sugeriu o encaminhamento do caso ao Ministério Público Estadual para apuração de possível improbidade administrativa, mas a recomendação não foi acolhida pelo relator.

A decisão ainda cabe recurso por parte da ex-gestora.

Os conselheiros da 2ª Câmara do Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios da Bahia decidiram, em sessão realizada na quarta-feira (08), acolher parcialmente uma denúncia contra o ex-prefeito de Brumado, Eduardo Lima Vasconcelos, envolvendo possíveis falhas em um processo licitatório voltado à área educacional. A relatoria ficou a cargo da conselheira Aline Peixoto, que determinou a aplicação de multa no valor de R$ 2 mil.

De acordo com informações divulgadas ao site Achei Sudoeste, a denúncia partiu de um conselheiro municipal do Fundeb e teve como foco o Pregão Presencial nº 31/2023. O certame previa um investimento estimado em R$ 7,3 milhões para a contratação de uma empresa responsável por desenvolver atividades complementares ao ensino nas escolas municipais de tempo integral.

Durante a análise, o tribunal identificou irregularidade na alteração do edital sem a reabertura do prazo legal, após mudança em um requisito relacionado à comprovação de capital social das empresas participantes. Na avaliação dos conselheiros, essa modificação poderia ter influenciado a elaboração das propostas e limitado a concorrência, comprometendo a lisura do processo.

Por outro lado, não foram confirmadas as alegações de favorecimento à empresa vencedora, já que não houve provas suficientes para sustentar essa acusação. Também foi considerada regular a participação de um dos sócios da empresa contratada, uma vez que ele não mantinha vínculo com a administração municipal no período da licitação.

text:
12 Chinese habits I wish I started in my 20s. I hate to say it, but my mom was right 😅

1. don’t go to bed with wet hair — wind and cold enter through the scalp and wreck your sleep quality and kidney qi over time. my mom warned me for years. she was right.

2. drink warm water, especially in the morning — cold water first thing shocks your digestive system. switching to warm water changed my gut within weeks.

3. keep your neck, belly button, and feet warm — these are major entry points for cold in TCM. cold feet = poor circulation = everything downstream suffers.

4. eat warm, cooked foods when you’re depleted — raw salads and cold smoothies take more energy to digest than they give back. soups and congee exist for a reason.

5. chew more, eat without screens — digestion starts in the mouth and your nervous system needs to be in rest mode to actually absorb what you’re eating.

6. incorporate herbal teas, soups and elixirs — ginger, red dates, goji, bone broth. food as medicine, not supplementation.

7. honor the 11pm–1am sleep window — this is when your liver and gallbladder are doing their deepest repair work. staying up past midnight is one of the fastest ways to deplete your system.

8. rest more during your luteal phase and period — your body is doing significant work. pushing through it costs more than you think.

9. swap some HIIT for gentle movement — walking, qi gong, yoga. high intensity when you’re already depleted spikes cortisol and deepens fatigue.

10. walk after meals — 10–15 minutes supports digestion, blood sugar, and mental clarity. 

11. notice your emotional patterns — in TCM, emotions live in specific organs. chronic worry, grief, stress — these aren’t just mental. they’re physical.

12. treat your cycle as information, not an inconvenience — pain, mood shifts, irregularity are your body communicating. once i started listening, everything shifted.

#tcm #chinese #lessonslearned

post_owner.name: Miko Wang
text:
My husband is a TCM doctor, so I make a lot of soups at home! Here’s my TCM-inspired chicken noodle soup using an Instant Pot.

Follow + comment “RECIPE” and I’ll send you the full steps 💌

Ingredients
• 1 whole free-range chicken or you can also use 10 chicken drumsticks 
• 5–6 red dates
• 3 dried shiitake mushrooms
• 3 slices ginger
• 5–6 cloves garlic
• 4 green onions (white parts only)
• 1 handful goji berries
• Somen noodles

Optional:
• Oyster mushrooms
• Beancurd (tofu skin or soft tofu)

Instructions
1. Clean the chicken and rub with salt. Gently massage, then rinse well.
2. Soak dried shiitake mushrooms in hot water for 10–15 minutes.
Don’t discard the soaking water — it adds so much flavor.
3. In the Instant Pot, add whole chicken, ginger, red dates, garlic, green onion,  soaked mushrooms + mushroom water.
4. Fill with water up to the MAX line.
5. Pressure cook on HIGH for 35 minutes.
6. Let it naturally release. Remove the chicken, shred the meat, and discard bones + aromatics. Skim off excess oil from the broth.
7. Turn on sauté mode and simmer for 15–20 minutes.
Add oyster mushrooms (optional) and goji berries.
8. Add beancurd (optional) and simmer for a few more minutes.
9. Cook somen noodles separately. 10. Season with salt to taste. Enjoy!! 

Stovetop version:
Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer for about 60–90 minutes until the chicken is tender. Then follow the same steps!

Vaihdevuodet nähdään länsimaisessa lääketieteessä pääasiassa hormonaalisena muutoksena, jossa estrogeenitasot laskevat. Oireita voidaan hoitaa esimerkiksi hormonikorvaushoidolla tai muilla lääkkeellisillä ratkaisuilla – usein hyvin tuloksin.

Kiinalaisessa lääketieteessä (TCM) näkökulma on laajempi. Kyse ei ole vain hormoneista, vaan kehon kokonaisvaltaisesta muutoksesta, jossa elinvoima, palautuminen ja sisäinen tasapaino ovat keskiössä.

TCM:n mukaan vaihdevuosiin liittyvät oireet kytkeytyvät erityisesti:

– Munuaisten Yin ja Jing – kehon palautumiskyky, nesteet ja “viilentävä” perusta
– Maksan Qi:n virtaus – stressi, tunteet ja kehon sisäinen liike
– Sydämen ja Shenin tasapaino – uni, levollisuus ja psyykkinen hyvinvointi

Kun Yin heikkenee ja kehon tasapaino muuttuu, tämä voi näkyä esimerkiksi:

– kuumina aaltoina ja yöhikoiluna
– unihäiriöinä
– mielialan vaihteluina tai levottomuutena
– kuivuutena
– väsymyksen ja ylivireyden vuorotteluna

Akupunktion näkökulmasta vaihdevuodet on vaihe, jossa keho tarvitsee tukea uuden tasapainon löytämiseen.

Akupunktio voi:
– rauhoittaa autonomista hermostoa
– tukea kehon omaa säätelyä
– parantaa unen laatua
– tasapainottaa lämmönsäätelyä
– vähentää stressiperäistä kuormitusta

text:
As Medical Doctor & expert in Chinese medicine, it’s nice to see both medicine systems increasingly agree on a similar direction - especially because skin problems rarely start on the skin and need a holistic focus. 

1. The gut-skin axis
Chinese medicine linked skin and digestion long ago. Western medicine now studies the microbiome, immune signalling, and the gut-skin connection more seriously.

2. Stress affects skin
Chinese medicine has long viewed emotional stress as relevant in skin disease. Western medicine now has psychodermatology, cortisol research, and neuroinflammation.

3. Sleep is treatment-relevant
Chinese medicine always treated sleep as part of repair. Western medicine now links poor sleep to barrier dysfunction, inflammation, and slower healing.

4. Same diagnosis, different treatment
Chinese medicine is highly pattern-based and individualised. Western medicine increasingly moves in the same direction through personalised medicine.

5. Skin is not just treated with creams
Chinese medicine rarely treats skin as a purely surface issue. Western medicine, too, often has to look beyond topical care — toward hormones, inflammation, digestion, stress physiology, or the nervous system.

We are prone to colds + flus, our lungs, bowels and respiratory tract are most vulnerable. Our skin & hair become drier…

🤍 1. Nourish your Lung Qi:
Autumn belongs to the Lung in TCM. The dry autumn air can deplete lung moisture, leading to dry skin, a dry cough or lowered immunity. Support your lungs by adding warm, white-coloured foods to your diet — think pear, daikon radish, white sesame and congee. And stay hydrated with warm drinks, teas etc.

🔥 2. Protect your Yang energy:
As the days shorten, your body starts conserving warmth — just like nature does. Keep your lower back, neck and belly covered in the cooler air, swap cold and raw foods for warm and cooked, and honour earlier bedtimes. This is especially important if you’re navigating endo, a fertility journey or postpartum recovery.

🌬️ 3. Honour the season of letting go:
The lungs (paired with the emotion of grief) regulate our capacity to release. Autumn gently asks us to let go — of what no longer serves us, of held tension, of the busy pace of summer. Breathwork, rest and acupuncture are beautiful ways to support your nervous system through this shift.

Your body is always in conversation with the season. 🍂 When we listen, real healing becomes possible.

text:
Follow @vivecachow for Mochi’s cancer journey ❤️‍🩹

Disclaimer: this is our personal experience, none of this is professional veterinary advice. 

Mochi’s diagnosis is Stage 3 B cell Lymphoma with a prognosis of 1-2 months without treatment. 

While Mochi isn’t doing Chemo, I learned from a professional that TCVM (Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine) and Chemo in treating cancer in theory work against each other. Chemo focuses on killing the cells, whereas TCVM works towards building up the immune system so the body can fight — although it is common to have TCVM support the Chemo process in helping minimise the side effects (should the Chemo route be your decision for your baby).

If you’re unfamiliar with the concept of TCM, our bodies have a life force (Qi) that flows through us. With herbs and acupuncture, it’s all about restoring the body from any imbalances. From my experience, it’s approached best as a preventative and consistently incorporated into your lifestyle. With this in mind, alongside Mochi’s steroids for palliative care, he was prescribed Chinese herbs that really target lymph nodes, as well as building his immune system and helping with any stagnation in the blood.

In terms of diet, cancer tends to cause a lot of inflammation in the body. So it’s best to avoid warming foods, and increase the intake of cooling foods (cucumbers, yoghurt, blueberries etc.)

Mochi seems to not mind the Chinese medicine even though it’s sooo bitter, he’s definitely my son 🤣

#tcm #dog #cancer #holisticvet #vet

post_owner.name: The Eastern Philosophy
text:
In Western nutrition, foods are often reduced to their macronutrients: protein, fat, caloric density. Classical Chinese medicine instead classifies them by functional qualities: thermal nature, directional tendency, and their effects on processes like nourishment, movement, and containment. The emphasis is not on composition, but on physiological action: how a food alters the state of the body.

Eggs boiled with walnut shell can be read in precisely these terms. The egg occupies a well-established place in dietary therapy as a substance that restores blood and fluids, while walnut is categorized as warm and Kidney-directed, used in conditions marked by cold and insufficiency. The shell contributes a slight astringing quality, less about tonification than about stabilizing what has been restored.

The result is not an “energy-boosting” food in the modern sense, but a deliberately restorative preparation, oriented toward states of continuous fatigue and depletion characterized by feeling cold and having insufficient recovery. Chinese medicine does not reduce foods to macronutrients because it is concerned less with what a food contains than with what it does: how it alters physiological processes, and how those effects change in relation to the rest of the system.

post_owner.name: The Eastern Philosophy
text:
Are you experiencing any of these? 🐉 Spring, in Chinese medicine, is not a vague season of renewal, but a period defined as the initiation of movement.

The classical text Huangdi Neijing (circa 200 BC) describes spring as the time when yang qi begins to arise and disperse outward. What had been stored and contained over winter starts to loosen, ascend, and circulate. This is why classical guidance emphasizes early rising, gentle movement, and avoiding constraint, not as lifestyle trends, but as ways of aligning with a seasonal physiological shift.

Importantly, this movement is not inherently smooth. Late Chinese imperial physicians repeatedly note that spring tends to produce two kinds of imbalance: one where movement is blocked (constraint, stagnation), and another where it becomes excessively upward (irritability, headaches, red eyes, poor sleep). What we might describe today as mood volatility or seasonal discomfort was historically understood as a problem of direction and regulation of qi.

This is also why the most characteristic spring formulas (such as Xiao Yao San and its modification Jia Wei Xiao Yao San) do not “detox” in any modern sense. They course what is constrained and clear what rises excessively, attempting to restore a more even distribution of movement rather than suppress it.

Diet follows the same logic. Classical dietary texts favor lighter, less cloying foods in spring, not for moral or aesthetic reasons, but because dense, greasy foods were thought to impede this seasonal movement, while excessive heat (alcohol, spice, late nights) could drive it upward too quickly.

What emerges across these sources is a consistent principle: spring is not about “starting over,” but about managing a surge of movement without letting it become either stuck or chaotic. Much of what is framed in the Western world as “spring wellness” flattens this into detox language. Historically in Chinese medicine, the concern was more specific and subtle: how to let things move without losing control of their direction 🌬️

A healthy DIY tea strainer! 🍊🍵 If you didn’t catch our past video about how aged orange peels in Chinese medicine are worth more than gold—Chen Pi, which we have recommended as a remedy for drying internal dampness and dispelling phlegm, is the peel of the Citrus reticulata Blanco orange. Chen Pi is much more fragrant than regular orange peel and has increased medicinal properties.

Chen Pi, translated as “aged peel,” is prepared with a special production technique involving soaking, drying, and aging for several years. This is a different herb in Chinese medicine, with more medicinal properties than fresh orange peel.

First appearing in the classical medical text Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, recorded between 206 BC-220 AD, Chen Pi has been used for thousands of years in Chinese medicine. It is most commonly recommended for digestive problems (which is why it’s an ingredient in our digestion-improving formulas Xiang Sha Liu Jun Wan and Bao He Wan). 

Chen Pi is also frequently blended with ripe Pu’er tea, as both Pu’er tea and Chen Pi are often recommended for those with stomach issues, and the light citrus fragrance complements ripe Pu’er’s mellow taste. Chen Pi also is one of the top herbs recommended to dry dampness and dispel phlegm, as well as to decrease nausea (making it popular for morning sickness) and relieve lung inflammation.

This herb also has other remarkable health properties:

In a 2022 review published in Molecules, Chen Pi was singled out as a novel anticancer agent: “studies have confirmed that [Chen Pi] and its active ingredients have inhibitory effects on cancer… [its] flavonoids have outstanding performance blocking the cancer cell cycle to resist proliferation.”

A 2021 pharmacology study concluded that Chen Pi may counteract liver injury—one of its flavonoids significantly inhibited AKT1 phosphorylation, mediating activation of pathways against liver injury.

A 2020 animal study showed that Chen Pi protects against chronic heart failure.

We offer Pu’er + Chen Pi tea discs on our site 🍵🍊

Pu’er is a fermented tea from Yunnan that has soared in popularity in recent years due to its unique taste and remarkable health benefits. The tea has long been hailed in Chinese materia medica for its curative properties. The 18th c Compendium of Materia Medica points to Pu’er as the best medicinal for aiding digestion. By contrast, teas like greens and oolongs are generally regarded as “cold” in TCM and unsuitable for those with poor digestion.

Modern clinical studies show that Pu’er can help synthesize fewer new fats while burning more stored body fat. A 2021 study found that its regulation of gut microbiome and digestive function was superior to unfermented teas. A 2018 study found Pu’er’s protective effect against ethanol alcohol to be superior to green tea. Apart from its digestive benefits, Pu’er has also been shown to have stronger anti-cancer effects and to be the most heart healthy of all teas due to its cholesterol lowering effects.

Our Pu’er tea resins are made from 2018 aged Menghai Pu’er, and each multi-flavor tin comes with 5 flavors—sticky rice, jasmine, rose, traditional ripe, and traditional raw—flavored only with natural botanicals (even our sticky rice tea is made from a plant indigenous to the Xishuangbanna Rainforest).

This ancient method of making tea resin was a lost art until very recently. Modern technology has now made it possible to recreate the carefully guarded, labor-intensive recipe of making tea resin that originated during the Tang Dynasty as a delicacy for the ruling classes, but was lost during the collapse of the Qing. We hope to revive this rare form of tea that is not only convenient, but uses only the highest quality whole leaf Pu’er, not inferior materials often used for tea bags.

Wenwan walnuts, aka hand therapy or fitness walnuts, are part health remedy, part status symbol. This practice originated in the Han Dynasty, creating a unique Chinese walnut wellness culture. Back in stock on our site! 🌰

Natural walnut is the most popular form in China, as their shape and texture can massage acupoints in the hand, while the movement helps improve cognitive function and physical dexterity. Since the palms and ten fingers of both hands are closely connected with the internal and external organs of the body, each organ of the body has a corresponding acupressure point on the hands. When the ten fingers move the fitness ball, this motion massages multiple parts of the palm, thereby stimulating multiple acupoints.

Walnut varieties specifically selected for this purpose are considered a collectible art prized by connoisseurs, and are known as wenwan walnuts. Picked when they are 7-8 years old, these are considered to have collectible value. Each pair of wenwan walnuts must have a consistent size, texture and weight, with a deep and defined texture. Wenwan walnuts are considered more valuable after many years of play, creating a shiny, smooth, and aged surface. After decades of play, a red, jade-like patina develops which is considered especially precious.

We offer hand therapy walnuts on our site, and each come as a pair inside a traditional brocade box, accompanied with a care kit (including oil, brush, and a two-sided cleaning pick). We have curated two walnut varieties that are the easiest to move in the hand (Four Towers and Tiger Head), and offer 3 sizes and a choice of polished or unpolished.

text:
9 Things I Wish I Knew About Mental Health in Perimenopause and Menopause, According to Traditional Chinese Medicine

1️⃣ Hormonal Shifts Affect More Than Just Your Period
In TCM, declining Kidney Yin and Blood during menopause can lead to symptoms like anxiety, irritability, and insomnia—long before your period fully stops.

2️⃣ Your Liver Influences Your Mood
The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and emotions. If Liver Qi stagnates (often from stress), it can trigger mood swings, anger, or depression.

3️⃣ Sleep Is Your First Medicine
Poor sleep depletes Heart Blood and disturbs the Shen (mind/spirit). Perimenopause often brings disrupted sleep, which amplifies emotional symptoms.

4️⃣ You’re Not Just ‘More Emotional’—Your Heart May Be Out of Balance
In TCM, the Heart houses the Shen. If the Heart is affected by Heat, Blood deficiency, or stagnation, it can manifest as anxiety, racing thoughts, or feeling unsettled.

5️⃣ Digestive Health Impacts Mental Health
A weakened Spleen leads to Dampness, which can cloud the mind and contribute to brain fog, fatigue, and low motivation.

6️⃣ Yin Nourishment Calms the Mind
Yin deficiency, common in menopause, can lead to restlessness, agitation, and night sweats that disturb sleep and mental clarity.

7️⃣ External Stress Hits Harder Now
Your resilience may feel lower. TCM sees this as a depletion of foundational energy (Kidney Jing), making recovery from stress slower and more emotionally draining.

8️⃣ You Might Feel Lonely or Untethered—and That’s a Spirit Imbalance
In Chinese medicine, feeling disconnected, isolated, or ungrounded can reflect a Heart or Kidney imbalance. It’s not just in your head—it’s in your Qi.

9️⃣ You’re Not Meant to Push Through This Alone
In TCM, menopause is a profound life shift—not a problem to fix, but a transition to be supported. Community, nourishment, rest, and gentle practices are key to protecting your mental health.

Save this for when you need a reminder that what you’re feeling is real—and there’s another way to navigate it.

Binnen de TCM wordt de spijsvertering gezien als de basis van gezondheid.

In de praktijk zie ik dat veel klachten ontstaan op het moment dat de Milt- en Maagfunctiekring overbelast raakt.
Denk aan een opgeblazen gevoel, aanhoudende vermoeidheid, huidproblemen of hormonale disbalans.

Wat vaak wordt onderschat, is hoe sterk onze dagelijkse gewoontes hier invloed op hebben.
De manier waarop we eten, de temperatuur van voeding en de snelheid waarmee we eten, bepalen in grote mate hoe goed het lichaam voeding kan transformeren en omzetten in Qi en Bloed.

Wanneer voeding te koud is, sterk bewerkt of gehaast wordt gegeten, vraagt dit meer van de spijsvertering.
Op de lange termijn zie je dat de Milt verzwakt en dat wat we binnen de TCM het “spijsverteringsvuur” noemen, minder krachtig wordt.

Daarom ligt de focus binnen de Chinese geneeskunde niet op ingewikkelde diëten, maar op eenvoudige, warme en goed verteerbare voeding die het lichaam ondersteunt.

Voeding die de Milt helpt om haar functie weer op te bouwen. 

In de praktijk werk ik daarom vaak met voedingsmiddelen die al eeuwenlang worden gebruikt om de spijsvertering te ondersteunen.

➡️Warme, gestoofde appel bijvoorbeeld, die zacht is voor de Maag en helpt om de darmen te ondersteunen.
➡️Bottenbouillon, rijk aan voedingsstoffen en licht verteerbaar, vaak ingezet bij herstel.
➡️En kruiden zoals venkel, die helpen om spanning en gasvorming in de buik te verminderen.

Wat al deze voedingsmiddelen met elkaar gemeen hebben, is dat ze het lichaam niet belasten, maar ondersteunen.

Binnen de TCM gaat het namelijk niet om restrictie. Een verstoorde spijsvertering herstelt niet door minder te eten of strenger te zijn,
maar door warmte, voeding en balans terug te brengen in het systeem.

Het zijn vaak juist de kleine dagelijkse gewoontes die op de lange termijn het grootste verschil maken.

Dit zijn waardevolle inzichten, maar zonder inzicht in jouw constitutie blijven het losse adviezen.

Wie wirkt sich
Überarbeitung auf die Nieren aus?

Die Essenz der Nieren, oder Jing, ist der Vorrat an Lebensenergie, mit dem wir inkarniert werden und den wir von unserer Mutter und unserem Vater erhalten haben. „Jing“ kann in jede Energie umgewandelt werden, die der Körper benötigt, Yin, Yang, Blut, Qi.

Außerdem speichern die Nieren den Willen, steuern die Knochen und sind mit dem Hören verbunden. Deshalb verschlechtert sich das Gehör mit zunehmendem Alter, denn mit dem Alter nimmt die Lebensenergie ab. Die Nieren stehen auch mit den Haaren auf dem Kopf in Verbindung. Dichtes Haar ist nicht nur schön, sondern auch ein Zeichen von Lebensenergie.

Wie kannst du die Essenz der Nieren stärken?

Wichtig ist zuerst, dass du aufhörst, dauerhaft gegen deinen Körper zu leben. Ständige Überarbeitung, zu wenig Regeneration und ein Alltag ohne Gleichgewicht schwächen auf Dauer dein System.

Was deine Nieren aus Sicht der TCM stärken kann:

• Qigong, um Energie aufzubauen, den Körper zu regulieren und die innere Ruhe zu fördern
• ein bewusster Alltag ohne ständige Überlastung
• ein Gleichgewicht zwischen geistiger Arbeit und körperlicher Aktivität
• regelmäßige Mahlzeiten über den Tag verteilt
• weniger spätes Essen am Abend
• Meditation, um dein Nervensystem zu beruhigen und innere Unruhe zu senken
• die Arbeit an Ängsten, denn Angst gilt in der TCM als die Emotion der Nieren
• Lebensmittel wie Brombeeren, Heidelbeeren und schwarze Bohnen

Auch Akupunktur kann dabei unterstützen, die Nieren wieder mehr ins Gleichgewicht zu bringen. Der Ansatz ist dabei immer individuell und ganzheitlich.

Manchmal beginnt Stärkung nicht mit noch mehr Tun, sondern mit weniger Raubbau an dir selbst. Mehr Rhythmus. Mehr Ruhe. Mehr Bewusstsein für das, was dein Körper jeden Tag trägt.

Woran merkst du selbst am schnellsten, dass dein Körper mehr Ruhe und Ausgleich braucht?

post_owner.name: Chee Hee | Chinese Medicine Practitioner🇲🇾
text:
Chinese Medicine does not ignore diagnosis. It just goes one step deeper.

Modern medicine helps us identify what the illness is.
Chinese Medicine asks: how is this illness showing up in this person?

Even when there is no clear cure, no simple fix, or no one-size-fits-all answer, Chinese Medicine can still offer support through pattern diagnosis.

We look beyond the label.
We look at the symptoms, the body’s signs, the pattern, and how the person is actually living through it.

Two people can have the same illness, but experience it in completely different ways. That is why pattern differentiation is so important. It helps us understand what kind of support a person needs, not just what name their illness has.

So even if a condition cannot be fully cured, there is still so much we can do to support better sleep, better digestion, less discomfort, more energy, and a better quality of life.

That is one of the biggest strengths of Chinese Medicine.

In mijn praktijk ontmoet ik veel mensen die al een hele weg hebben afgelegd in hun gezondheid.

Ze hebben zich verdiept in voeding, bewuster leren eten en geprobeerd beter voor hun lichaam te zorgen, en toch blijft er vaak een gevoel aanwezig dat het lichaam niet volledig meebeweegt, dat de Qi niet vrij stroomt en dat de spijsvertering niet doet wat ze ervan verwachten.

Wanneer ik met iemand meekijk vanuit de TCM, kom ik vaak uit bij de Milt- en Maagfunctiekring, omdat deze aan de basis liggen van het vormen van Qi en Bloed en daarmee van hoe iemand zich dagelijks voelt.

Wanneer deze functiekring uit balans raakt, zie je dat de transformatie en transportfunctie van de Milt minder efficiënt verloopt, waardoor voeding minder goed wordt omgezet en er geleidelijk Damp kan ontstaan. 

Dit proces is vaak subtiel en ontwikkelt zich over tijd, maar wordt voelbaar in het lichaam als zwaarte, vermoeidheid, een opgeblazen gevoel of een gebrek aan helderheid.

Ook de aard van voeding speelt hierin een belangrijke rol. De Milt heeft een voorkeur voor warmte en regelmaat, en reageert op een rustige, zachte manier wanneer voeding goed bereid en afgestemd is. 

Wanneer voeding te koud, te rauw of te belastend is voor het systeem, vraagt dit meer van de Qi en wordt het voor het lichaam moeilijker om balans te behouden.

Wat ik in de begeleiding steeds opnieuw zie, is dat er rust ontstaat wanneer iemand zijn of haar eigen patroon begint te herkennen. Wanneer duidelijk wordt hoe Qi beweegt, hoe Bloed wordt opgebouwd en waar stagnatie of Damp zich heeft ontwikkeld, ontstaat er richting.

Vanuit die richting kan het lichaam stap voor stap ondersteund worden, met voeding, kruiden en leefstijl die passen bij dat specifieke systeem.

Dit is geen proces van snelle oplossingen, maar van afstemming en begrip.

Wanneer je je lichaam op deze manier leert kennen, verandert niet alleen hoe je je voelt, maar ook hoe je met je gezondheid omgaat.

Als je voelt dat je hier dieper naar wilt kijken en wilt begrijpen wat er in jouw lichaam speelt, kun je me een bericht sturen met CONSTITUTIE.

post_owner.name: The Eastern Philosophy
text:
The tiniest pills in traditional Chinese medicine, this is a 40+ year old vessel 🌿 Liuying Wan (六应丸) is a discreet powerhouse of classical Chinese herbal medicine—long revered for its effectiveness in treating tonsillitis, sore throats, and early-stage glandular swellings. Often prescribed for “clearing heat” in the throat and lymphatic regions, the formula works by rapidly reducing inflammation.

What makes Liuying Wan especially striking is its size. Traditionally, these were packaged in thumb-sized glass vials—barely larger than a fingertip—containing dozens of tiny, pearl-like pills, each no bigger than a grain of millet. But the size is not incidental. In fact, it reflects a key tenet of Chinese medical formulation: potency through precision.

The micro-dosage allows for several things:
➤ Sublingual or buccal absorption, targeting the upper respiratory and throat tissues directly
➤ Ease of titration, enabling practitioners to scale doses according to the patient’s constitution and stage of illness
➤ Minimal digestive burden, making it especially suitable for children or those with GI issues.

Historically, these miniature forms were also easier to preserve and transport, often carried in silk pouches or scholar’s kits. Each tiny sphere was hand-rolled, then covered with medicinal glazes or plant resins to preserve freshness. Many of the Chinese medicine formulas we carry continue to use traditional tiny pills, known as “tea pills,” which are easier than tablets or pills to dissolve in the stomach and digest.

This artifact is a testament that in traditional Chinese medicine, efficacy doesn’t always come in large doses. Sometimes, it’s the smallest pills that carry the most refined thought ☯️

Have you ever come across this format of medicine? 🍃

post_owner.name: Jeremy Cornish
text:
Here's the big mistake acupuncturists make, in one sentence:

"Acupuncture doesn't hurt"

This is so risky. Best case you're right and the patient doesn't feel any pain. In terms of trust/relationship building you're breaking even.

However, if it does hurt, there is now cognitive dissonance between what you said and what they feel. This is the thin edge of the axe coming into your patient-practitioner relationship.

"Oh Jeremy I don't have to listen to you because my needle technique is so advanced/smooth/gentle that it really doesn't ever hurt"

Congrats. However please remember that we don't get to decide what our patients classify as pain.

Even a proper de qi, or a heavy feeling, or a bit of warmth, or a light tingle...

Any of these can be new sensations for people. And our subconscious tends to throw a negative lens over novelty as a protective mechanism.

We can very easily classify new sensations as "pain"

So do you really want to argue with your new patient when they say it hurts?

Much better to open the doors of communication into a process:

"Does acupuncture hurt?"

"Not usually but if you feel anything you're not sure about let me know so I can adjust it"

It's not about answering the question, it's about answering in a way that keeps you connected, keeps them empowered over what they're going to be experiencing, and creates more room for trust, not less.

It puts you on their team, and helps them stay in control over the process.

As you get better at this we move up a level from a conversation about methods to problems/goals. 

"Does acupuncture hurt?"

"It might. Does that matter if it helps you achieve your goal?"

Different types of people will respond better to those frames...

Patient communication is one of the least developed and most powerful skills we can have.

Without these skills we're more likely to have no shows, people dropping off the schedule, unfinished treatment plans, less referrals, volatile cash flow...

Your first show will not be your best. Your conditioning will probably not be perfect. Your posing will need work. You will make mistakes in your prep that you will only understand in hindsight.

None of that matters as much as you think it does right now.

What your first show actually does has very little to do with where you place. It forces you to find out what you are made of over a sustained period of time. Not a good week or a few months of in and out progress. Months of consistent, unglamorous, daily discipline when you’re not in the mood, hunger, and self-doubt.

Most people never find that out about themselves. 

It also gives you a baseline. A real, honest reference point for everything that follows. Before your first show, you are guessing at what your body can do, what your mind can handle, and what prep can actually pull from you. After it, you know. And that experience changes the way you train, the way you eat, and the way you approach every goal you set from that point forward.

The clients I have coached who took their first show seriously, regardless of the result, came back for their second prep with a completely different level of clarity and commitment. Not because they won. But because they went through something that most people are not willing to go through, and they came out the other side knowing exactly what they needed to work on.

That is not something you can teach. It is not something you can learn from watching someone else do it. You have to do it yourself.

If you have been sitting on this decision, I am not going to tell you it is easy or that the timing will ever feel perfect. It will not be.

Benefits: Gua sha stimulates microcirculation, reduces inflammation, enhances the immune system, and provides pain relief for conditions like tension headaches, neck pain, and back pain.

Treatment Areas: While popular for facial rejuvenation and lymphatic drainage (using lighter pressure), it is commonly used on the back, shoulders, and neck for therapeutic purposes.

In essence, Gua Sha is a “therapeutic purging” method used to restore the smooth flow of blood and energy, resolving the underlying causes of pain. Try it yourself, I promise you won’t regret it! Oh and want to know why my skin is so good? DM me to find out 🤗

text:
Are you wondering why I’m balancing eggs?

This playful (and frustrating!) ritual actually comes from an ancient Chinese tradition, practiced for over 4,000 years during Chunfen, the Spring Equinox and during Spring.

It’s believed that if you can balance an egg on this day, it will bring good luck, prosperity and harmony for the year ahead.

In Chinese culture, the egg is a powerful symbol of new life, fertility and renewal. So when nature itself is perfectly balanced ,when day and night are equal, people try to stand eggs upright, marking the shift into a new season of growth and possibility.

There’s also a long-held idea that the unique alignment of the Earth and sun on the equinox makes this easier… although I’ve not managed it yet!

I love this ritual, because really, who doesn’t want more luck? And it’s a lovely reminder that Spring has arrived.

We’ve made this tea for many of our pregnant guests at the studio, using our organic / garden herbs! And today we’d like to share with you. This is a very safe and gentle tea for morning sickness, safe for pregnancy. 

💕Recipe (one day serving):

- 30g of toasted rice (or brown rice / buckwheat / millet)
- 8g dried shiso leaves or 30g fresh
- 1-3 jujube dates to taste 
- 15g dried ginger or 40g fresh 
- water (less water for stronger taste, more for lighter taste) 
- Boil for 10 minutes, steep for 20 mins.

O Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios do Pará (TCMPA) homologou, nesta terça-feira (17), uma medida cautelar que determina a suspensão dos pagamentos relacionados à obra de reforma do Canal São Joaquim, em Belém. A decisão visa resguardar recursos públicos após a identificação de falhas na execução do projeto.

A medida, inicialmente concedida pelo conselheiro Cezar Colares e relatada em plenário pelo presidente da Corte, Lúcio Vale, suspende os repasses do Contrato nº 13/2024, firmado entre a Prefeitura de Belém e a Secretaria Municipal de Zeladoria e Conservação Urbana (Sezel), até nova deliberação.

De acordo com relatório técnico do tribunal, a fiscalização apontou uma série de irregularidades, como aditivos contratuais considerados ilegais, alterações no projeto sem formalização, problemas nas fundações da obra, atrasos no cronograma e pagamentos incompatíveis com o andamento dos serviços.

A situação ganhou maior gravidade após a interdição de um trecho da Avenida Júlio César, motivada pelo risco de queda de uma passarela ligada à obra. Segundo o tribunal, o problema representa risco à população e reforçou a necessidade de intervenção imediata.

Foraging wild mushrooms

The Yin to the Yang

Because we have to live our medicine, which means respecting balance

So that we can slow down

How do you live more slowly?

post_owner.name: Rádio São Francisco 97.7 FM
text:
Uma decisão do Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios de Goiás (TCM-GO) proibiu a Prefeitura de Anápolis de firmar novos contratos emergenciais para a gestão do Hospital Municipal Alfredo Abrahão.

O acórdão nº 01544/2026, publicado na terça-feira (17), também determinou que o atual vínculo com a Fundação Universitária Evangélica, a Funev, não seja prorrogado.

Segundo o tribunal, houve irregularidade na sucessão de contratos emergenciais, iniciados durante a gestão Roberto Naves (Republicanos) e renovados em 2025, que somaram 18 meses de gestão sem licitação, em desacordo com a Lei nº 14.133/2021.

A prática foi considerada inadequada por contrariar o caráter excepcional desse tipo de contratação.

A decisão, no entanto, não impede a Funev de participar de um novo processo licitatório regular.

🗣️ TCM exige licitação

O que o TCM-GO veda é a continuidade de contratações emergenciais, exigindo que a gestão municipal conclua o chamamento público aberto ainda em 2024 para selecionar, de forma competitiva, a organização social responsável pela unidade.

O relator do caso, conselheiro Daniel Goulart, teve parecer seguido pelo plenário ao apontar a necessidade de regularização imediata do modelo de gestão.

Com isso, o prefeito Márcio Corrêa (PL) e a gestora do Fundo Municipal de Saúde, Eliane Pereira dos Santos, terão prazo de 60 dias para apresentar um cronograma de conclusão do processo e documentos que comprovem a contratação regular.

A medida busca encerrar o ciclo de vínculos precários e garantir maior transparência e competitividade na escolha da entidade gestora do hospital.

📝 Samih Zakzak
📷 Victor Santos

• 3 snow fungus 🍄

text:
🍲 Eating from a TCM perspective isn’t just about what you eat… it’s about how you eat.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, your digestion is the foundation of your energy (Qi), blood, and overall health.

Your Spleen + Stomach = your digestive engine
If this system is weak → fatigue, bloating, dampness, brain fog

Here are 6 key ways to support it daily:

1️⃣ Eat warm, cooked foods
Your Spleen dislikes cold. Cold foods slow digestion and create dampness (bloating, heaviness, mucus).
👉 Think soups, stews, teas — not iced drinks and constant raw foods.

2️⃣ Eat at regular times
Your body runs on a rhythm, eating randomly = weak digestion over time.
🕖 7–9am (Stomach) receives
🕘 9–11am (Spleen) transforms

3️⃣ Eat calmly (this one is BIG)
Stress disrupts digestion. In TCM: Liver Qi stagnation “attacks” the Spleen. Avoid working and screen time simultaneously. Bring JOY into this eating.

4️⃣ Match food to your body
There’s no “one diet fits all” in TCM. Food = daily medicine.
Feeling cold + tired → need warming foods
Feeling heaty, inflamed → need cooling support
Feeling heavy + sluggish → reduce dampness

5️⃣ Avoid too much cold + fluids with meals
Too much liquid (especially cold) = “dilutes digestive fire”. This slows breakdown and weakens your system over time.

6️⃣ Stop at 70–80% full
Overeating → food stagnation → dampness. That heavy, sleepy, bloated feeling after eating? That’s your Spleen struggling.

🌸You are not just what you eat — you are what your body can transform.

🌸Support your digestion, and everything else becomes easier: energy, hormones, immunity, clarity.

If this resonates, start simple:  warm meals, regular timing, slow down when you eat

En la tradición clásica fue considerado tan potente que algunos médicos decían que con este punto se podían tratar casi todas las enfermedades 🤯

✅️ Porque Zusanli regula el eje central del cuerpo: Estómago y Bazo.

En medicina china, estos órganos son responsables de transformar los alimentos en Qi y Sangre, la energía que literalmente sostiene la vida.

Por eso este punto es famoso por:

⚡ Fortalecer el Qi
🩸 Nutrir la Sangre
🌿 Fortalecer Bazo y Estómago
🔥 Regular el Yangming (capa con igual cantidad de Qi y Sangre)
🧠 Calmar el Shen

text:
This is one of the most common formats of traditional Chinese medicine. These wax balls, containing “wan” or a round herbal ball inside, vary in size from as large as an egg to the size of a mustard seed.

Traditionally, honey was the binding substance in the pill-making process, layered with medicinal herb powder, and the medicine sealed on the outside with an airtight wax coating. This was considered the most durable method for storing herbal medicine without the need for preservatives.

There is evidence that this innovation dates back 2,000 years, as wax was found to be used for similar purposes in an ancient Chinese tomb. However, it has largely been replaced with all-plastic bottles in modern medicine. We still offer a few herbal medicines encased in wax, including Die Da Wan for injury healing and Baifeng Wan for women’s health.

Note: other herbal medicine formulas also comes in this ball format, also known as a honey bolus. This does not mean they are the same medicine. For example, the one shown is for emergency situations such as strokes and heart attack. However, almost every possible herbal formula in Chinese medicine has been made in this same form, including the two mentioned above that we carry (for injuries and period cramps).

Have you ever come across this format of medicine? 🍃
