Traditional Chinese Medicine is blowing up on TikTok right now, and honestly…we are HERE for it! 👏👏👏

So much of TCM revolves around warmth. And during cold weather like this, supporting warmth, circulation, and digestion matters even more.

Here are three very practical ways to start incorporating these principles this week:

1. Prioritize warm foods and drinks

This might sound unusual, but soup for breakfast is common in many cultures and incredibly supportive for digestion! Warm lemon or apple water in the morning, soups, stews, and cooked foods help wake up digestion far more gently than cold smoothies or iced drinks.

2. Always keep your feet warm

Cold floors pull heat from the body. Keeping house shoes or slippers visible and easy to grab helps make this habit automatic. No bare feet around here, especially during cold months.

3. Slow down when you eat

Put your fork down between bites. Take a breath before your first bite. Sit down and eat without scrolling. These small shifts help signal safety to your nervous system and allow digestion to actually do its job.

text:
Today I’m sharing two commonly used antiviral herbs you’ll often see in shops like this
Banlangen and Gan Mao Ling.

These can be helpful for short term, acute situations like the very beginning of a cold or viral exposure. They’re part of the reason people are drawn to Chinese medicine in the first place.

That said, this is where I want to slow things down for a moment.

In the West, we’re very used to the idea that if something works, it works fast. Take a pill, symptoms stop, job done. Chinese medicine doesn’t work like that.

This medicine is about formulas, precision, and time. It’s about actually addressing what’s happening in the body, not just silencing symptoms. These single herbs or patent formulas can be supportive in small moments, but they are not a replacement for proper diagnosis or treatment.

If you’re dealing with chronic illness, frequent infections, long term inflammation, or something that keeps coming back, this is where working with a trained practitioner matters.

Always speak to the staff in these shops before picking things up, and if you need real support, that’s what I’m here for.

This series was about opening the door to Chinese medicine, not self diagnosing.

And yes, Lily is still our absolute gem. We adore her. 🫶🏼

Link is in my bio to book a consultation and let’s figure out what’s actually going on.

In face reading, vertical lines speak to experience —
what has been lived, carried, integrated, or held through time.

Horizontal lines tend to reflect age and cycles of time.
Vertical lines tell a different story.

They form when life asks something of you
and the body adapts to keep moving forward.

That’s why the 11 lines

often appear together.

Both can reflect digestion and elimination in the body,

Experience leaves direction.

post_owner.name: Gavin Larsen | TCM Hair Loss Practitioner
text:
This happened to me for 3 years.

Ferritin: 42 ng/mL. Doctor said “normal” (range 12-150). 

Vitamin D: 36 ng/mL. Doctor said “sufficient” (range >30). 

TSH: 3.4 mIU/L. Doctor said “perfect” (range 0.5-4.5).

Still losing 100+ hairs daily.

Then I learned the difference between “normal” and “optimal for hair growth.”

Research shows hair needs different thresholds:

Ferritin: “Normal” >15 ng/mL (prevents anemia) Optimal 70-100 ng/mL for active regrowth

Vitamin D: “Normal” >30 ng/mL Optimal 50-80 ng/mL for follicle cycling

TSH: “Normal” 0.5-4.5 mIU/L Optimal <2.5 mIU/L for sustained anagen phase

Hair follicles are non-essential tissue. Your body prioritizes heart, brain, vital organs.

If ferritin is barely adequate for survival functions, there’s nothing left for hair growth.

Pattern 2 connection: If you’re supplementing but ferritin won’t rise, you have an absorption issue—low stomach acid, gut inflammation, or malabsorption.

Fix digestion BEFORE loading more iron. Otherwise supplements pass through undigested.

Your doctor prevents disease. I optimize function. Both are necessary. Only one grows hair.

👉🏼 Comment “PATTERN” if your doctor says everything’s “normal” but you’re still losing 100+ hairs daily—optimal ≠ normal.

text:
❓Ist dir schon aufgefallen, dass dein Kind nachts immer wieder zu ganz bestimmten Uhrzeiten aufwacht?

Gerade in emotional intensiven Phasen – wie einer Eingewöhnung – passiert das besonders häufig.

💡In der Traditionellen Chinesischen Medizin (TCM) wird der Schlaf als Teil eines nächtlichen Energiezyklus gesehen. Bestimmte Organe sind zu festen Zeiten besonders aktiv. 
👉🏼 Wenn Kinder emotional viel verarbeiten, ist ihr Schlaf oft leichter – und genau in diesen Zeitfenstern wachen sie schneller auf.

🇨🇳 So erklärt die TCM diese Uhrzeiten:

🕚 23:00 Uhr – Gallenblase
Diese Phase steht für Anpassung und emotionale Stabilität. Viele Kinder reagieren hier sensibel auf Veränderungen wie z.B Licht oder Geräusche. Deshalb wachen viele Kinder auf, wenn ihre Eltern selbst schlafen gehen.
👉🏼 Tipp: Etwas früher oder später ins Bett gehen und wenig Geräusche in dieser Zeit machen. 

🕐 01:00 Uhr – Leber
Die Leber ist in der TCM mit Stress- und Emotionsverarbeitung verbunden. Eindrücke des Tages können jetzt „nachhallen“.
👉🏼 Tipp: Abends Tempo rausnehmen und ganz viel Nähe anbieten.

🕒 03:00 Uhr – Lunge
Diese Phase steht für Loslassen und innere Verarbeitung. Viele Kinder brauchen genau jetzt zusätzliche Sicherheit durch Nähe.
👉🏼 Tipp: Sanfte Berührung und ganz viel Kuscheln helfen hier am Besten. 

🕔 05:00 Uhr – Darm & Aufwachhormone
Der Körper schaltet langsam in den „Morgenmodus“: Cortisol steigt an, die Verdauung beginnt zu arbeiten, der Schlaf wird leichter.
👉🏼 Tipp: passender Schlafzeitpunkt am Abend für ausreichender Schlafdruck auch am Morgen und in den frühen Morgenstunden Licht und Geräusche gering halten.

‼️ Wichtig: Das ist kein medizinisches Urteil, sondern ein traditioneller Blickwinkel. Gerade während emotional aufregenden Zeiten (wie bei uns aktuell mit der Kita Eingewöhnung) zeigt häufiges nächtliches Aufwachen nicht, dass etwas falsch läuft – sondern dass dein Kind gerade viel zu verarbeiten hat. 

💾 Speichere dir den Beitrag für genau solche Zeiten.

Your ancestors knew: 

Winter is for building, storing, and conserving. Not depleting.

"You're trying to be nice and you're hurting your patients"

That's what my supervisor told me in the student clinic in 2007.

He playfully expanded on this point through his thick Chinese accent:

"You see alot of patterns and you're trying to treat them all at once. You're trying to be nice but it's a messy herb formula trying to do everything. You have to pick one thing and work on that first"

This was sagely (and much needed) advice at the time.

And he really got me thinking. But what was missing at the time was a way to pick...

If we see hidden pathogens, dampness, heat, qi stagnation, blood stasis, qi deficiency and a bit of yin deficiency...

How do we pick?

Ten years later I found my answer.

The human body is a system of systems and has an order of operations when it comes to healing.

So all the patterns you see aren't flat with equal weighting.

In fact the sooner we learn which ones to emphasize and which to ignore, the sooner we start making a real difference for complex cases.

Because when you get the right patterns first they start to undo the others. 

Often times with the right approach 3-4 of the secondary patterns will fall away within a few weeks. You'll be left with a much more straightforward clinical picture.

As we get better at this type of thinking we become more effective (of course) and also way more efficient. Office visits that used to take 30 minutes now take 5. 

It can freak you out at first. But when you start seeing through the matrix code you don't have to ask 10,000 questions any more.

text:
Not all Kinesiology courses are the same...and that’s okay.

As long as you do your due diligence if you are a prospective student and know what you are signing up for.

Unfortunately I have had a lot of kinesiology students contact me over the years who come to me feeling disheartened, lost, disappointed and frustrated and are at the point of giving up on their passion because their kinesiology training was not what they thought it was going to be.

As a prospective student you need to ask all the questions.
Kinesiology is not a regulated industry and it has changed a lot since I started my journey nearly 2 decades ago when there were only a couple of places in Melbourne to study.

Questions I would recommend asking yourself are:
‘What kind of practitioner do I want to be?’
‘Am I looking for a career change?’
‘Is this only for my own self development?’
‘Do I want to build a kinesiology business and have longevity in
the industry?’
‘Am I interested in just short courses and 1 year of study or do I want the option of studying for 2,3 or even 4 years to become a master practitioner one day?’

Questions I would recommend asking any potential school/ teacher:
‘Why do you teach the kinesiology modality that you do?’
‘What inspires you to inspire others on this journey?’ 
‘What is the point of difference with the kind of kinesiology you teach?’ (The person should be able to answer this without talking with ill will of another school/course/teacher)
‘What are your qualifications to teach and how long have you been teaching?’
‘Why should I come and learn from you?’

text:
❤️Ginseng Chicken Tonic for Fatigue and Stress

If you’ve been feeling tired but wired and never well rested, burnt out, dry inside from winter heating, or just running on empty, this is one of the most supportive TCM soups you can make. This is a gentle tonic that restores Qi and Yin at the same time while calming internal heat and supporting digestion. Perfect for:

✨ burnout & overworking
✨ dry throat or dry cough
✨ “tired but wired” stress
✨ mild deficiency heat
✨ winter dryness from indoor heating
✨ recovery after illness
✨ postpartum week 3–4 (after heat clears)

It’s clear, slightly sweet, gently cooling-but-nourishing — the kind of quiet, steady support your body feels immediately.

Ingredients:
🍗 5-6 fresh chicken drumsticks – strengthen Spleen Qi for steady energy
🌿 1-2 fresh American/Canadian ginseng (花旗参) – nourishes Yin, cools deficiency heat, supports mental clarity
🐚 10 dried scallops (乾瑤柱) – deepen the umami and strengthen Spleen + Kidney
❤️ 10 dried red dates (紅棗) – nourish Blood, harmonize the formula
🍇 10 dried red goji berries (枸杞) – moisten dryness + support Liver/Kidney Yin
🤍 Fresh Chinese yam (淮山)– tonifies Qi + Yin and supports digestion
💧 2 L of water

In your pot (I’m using a ceramic pot), you can panfry the chicken drumsticks to brown them for more flavour. Once that’s browned, add in 2L of water and bring that to a boil. Once that boils, add in your American ginseng, scallops, goji berries, red dates, and Chinese yam and boil covered for another 2 hours on medium heat (gentle bubbling). Salt gently to taste.

⚠️ Who Should Avoid This Soup?

Because American ginseng is cooling, skip this soup if you have:
• cold hands/feet or loose stools
• Spleen/Kidney Yang deficiency
• active cold/flu symptoms
• dampness or phlegm
• very weak digestion

🌸You can find the full recipe here: https://thechinesesouplady.com/ginseng-chicken-tonic-for-fatigue-and-stress/

text:
🤧Just had a cold? Here’s what not to do unless you want it to come back, according to Traditional Chinese medicine.

Here are five things I tell patients not to do right after a cold virus. These may seem small, but in both Western and Chinese medicine, your recovery period matters. This is when your body rebuilds strength, clears remaining pathogens, and restores immune balance. What you do during this window can either support a full recovery or lead to lingering symptoms, fatigue, or relapse.

1. Do not jump back into intense exercise.
Even if your energy feels okay, your immune system is still recalibrating. Pushing yourself too hard with workouts can drive lingering pathogens deeper and increase your chances of post-viral fatigue, chronic cough, or inflammation.

2. Do not expose yourself to cold or wind.
This includes cold weather, air conditioning, fans, wet hair, or open necklines. In Chinese medicine, “wind” is not just weather. It is a common way illness re-enters the body when your system is vulnerable and still recovering.

3. Do not skip meals or eat cold, raw foods.
Smoothies, salads, iced drinks, and protein bars ask too much of your digestion while you are healing. After a virus, digestion is often weaker. Warm, cooked, and simple meals help rebuild your strength and restore the fluids lost during illness.

4. Do not go back to late nights.
Sleep is critical after a virus. Staying up late can prevent your body from fully clearing out what remains and increases the risk of relapse or lingering symptoms. Sleep supports immune recovery.
5. Do not assume the illness is fully gone just because symptoms have improved.

In Chinese medicine, recovery continues even after obvious symptoms resolve. This is the window where the right care can prevent sinus infections, lingering cough, immune crashes, or even autoimmune flares.

Think of the days after a cold as a quiet rebuilding phase, not a finish line.

If this resonates, save it. If you know someone who always gets sick again after a cold, share this with them.

O Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios da Bahia (TCM-BA) suspendeu o pregão eletrônico que previa a contratação de empresas para fornecimento de trios elétricos para o Carnaval de Juazeiro (BA). A suspensão abrange trios de pequeno, médio e grande porte.

O conselheiro e relator do processo Nelson Pellegrino acatou denúncia apresentada por uma empresa. O edital foi suspenso dois dias após a publicação. 

Entre as supostas irregularidades apontadas estão a obrigatoriedade de registro das empresas no Conselho Regional de Química (CRQ), sem relação com o objeto da contratação. Segundo o TCM-BA, a cláusula não tem pertinência com serviços de trio elétrico e tende a afastar potenciais concorrentes. Além disso, o relatou também destacou a falha na ampliação da verificação de sanções administrativas a sócios majoritários das empresas, além da exigência de certidões negativas em nome desses sócios – condição não prevista na legislação de licitações.

O que diz a Prefeitura

“Tão logo haja a ciência oficial do teor do pronunciamento e das eventuais retificações apontadas, a administração adotará, de forma imediata, todas as providências cabíveis, em estrita observância aos princípios da legalidade, da transparência, da eficiência e do interesse público.

Ressalta-se, ainda, que a interposição de recursos pelas empresas participantes constitui prerrogativa expressamente prevista na legislação que rege os procedimentos licitatórios, a qual é integralmente respeitada pelo Município. A prefeitura reitera que todo o certame foi conduzido com rigor técnico e jurídico, em conformidade com as normas legais e regulamentares aplicáveis, mantendo-se comprometida com a regularidade, a lisura e a segurança jurídica dos atos administrativos”, diz a nota da Prefeitura de Juazeiro.

post_owner.name: Bandeirantes Goiânia
text:
O Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios de Goiás (TCM-GO) decidiu, por 6 votos a 1, suspender de forma cautelar o acórdão que enquadrava a Comurg como empresa estatal dependente da Prefeitura de Goiânia. Com isso, a companhia retoma provisoriamente a autonomia financeira ao longo de 2026, até o julgamento das contas do exercício.

📌 A decisão revoga temporariamente o entendimento adotado em abril de 2024, ainda na gestão do ex-prefeito Rogério Cruz, que incorporava as despesas da Comurg às contas do município, com reflexos diretos na Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal (LRF).

🗳️ O voto vencedor foi do presidente do TCM-GO, Joaquim de Castro, que considerou novos documentos e informações apresentadas pela empresa e pelo Executivo, apontando reestruturação administrativa e recuperação financeira. Segundo ele, a condição de estatal dependente deve ser analisada ano a ano, e a execução imediata da decisão anterior poderia gerar impactos relevantes e risco de descumprimento da LRF.

💬 O conselheiro Laécio do Amaral acompanhou o voto e destacou medidas adotadas em 2025, como a negociação com a PGFN, que representa quase R$ 2 bilhões de economia.

❗ O voto contrário foi do conselheiro Francisco Ramos, que questionou o procedimento. A maioria, porém, sustentou a decisão com base no poder geral de cautela.

🏛️ Durante a sessão, o prefeito Sandro Mabel detalhou ações de reestruturação:

✅R$ 189 milhões de redução no custo operacional fixo

✅Passivo com a PGFN reduzido de R$ 2,227 bilhões para R$ 312 milhões

✅Redução de R$ 520,4 milhões em ações trabalhistas, cíveis e tributárias

📄 No pedido de revisão, a Comurg alegou erro na caracterização de sua natureza jurídica, defendendo que os recursos do município são pagamentos por serviços, e não subvenções.

Why Chinese baddies don’t shower in the morning.
From traditional Chinese medicine perspective, morning is when your body’s energy is just starting to rise. That energy is still unstable and easy to disturb. So if you take a long or cold shower in the morning, your pores open too fast. This  can drain your energy, let cold and dampness into your body, and leave you feeling tired, foggy or even cold all day.
If you do shower in the morning, here are a few tips:
1. Use warm water, not cold.
2. Keep it short, 5-10 mins.
3. Wash your hair last.
4. Dry off immediately and stay warm.
And if you often feel low energy or cold, save your shower for the evening instead.

text:
Save this easy Chinese red date tea recipe ☕️ I get painful heavy periods and my mum taught me to make this quick and easy traditional Chinese red date ginger tea that helps to relieve cramping, replenish blood, improve circulation, reduce inflammation and give a boost in energy… and It’s all completely natural and caffeine free!

The red dates, or jujubes, are full of antioxidants and help with replenishment particularly after heavy periods. Sliced ginger helps to relieve cramping, bloating and aid digestion. Dried longan, a type of fruit in Asia, give sweetness and is packed with iron and vitamin C, then finally some goji berries also adds sweetness and help to reduce inflammation.

YOU WILL NEED:
 
- 10-12 red dates/jujube
- Fresh ginger, sliced
- 1 small handful of dried longan (approx 12-15)
- 1 small handful of goji berries
- 1-1.5 tsp brown sugar/rock sugar 
- 800ml water 

1. Carefully remove the pits of the jujube/red dates.
2. Add it into a bowl along with sliced ginger, dried longan and goji berries.
3. Give it a thorough wash and drain. Leave the goji berries and red dates to soak for 10-15 minutes to remove impurities, wash and drain.
4. Add the tea mix into a pot of water and bring to a boil on high heat.
5. Add brown sugar or rock sugar, mix and reduce to a medium low heat. Boil for another 15-20 minutes.
6. Serve and enjoy!

I like to drink this throughout my cycle, particularly a week before and after my period and you can get everything at an Asian supermarket!

- Sweet foods (soda, desserts, candy)

That dampness can travel upward to the Lungs and turn into phlegm, making your cough wetter, stickier, and heavier in the chest.

Cold constricts circulation and weakens Lung Qi. 
 
Whether it’s iced drinks or exposure to cold air, cold makes it harder for the Lungs to disperse fluids—often worsening coughs almost immediately.

Spicy foods create heat and dryness. 
 
Since the Lungs prefer a moist environment, excess heat dries them out, turning a mild cough into a dry, scratchy, and painful one.
 
- Fried food
 
Fried foods generate both heat and phlegm at the same time. 
 
This combination makes mucus thicker and harder to expel, often increasing phlegm even when you’re not actively coughing.

- Seafood
 
In Chinese Medicine, seafood is considered a triggering food, especially for inflammatory or allergic conditions. 
 
It can aggravate coughing, asthma, and skin issues by stimulating internal wind and inflammation.

I came home last night with a small cough and made this immediately. Next morning, cough was barely there! Made it again today and even did a hard trainer ride without coughing! Will make one more tomorrow and hopefully, it’s gone! AMAZING! ❤️

🔻Opens the lungs and eases breathing
🔻Supports digestion & reduces bloating
🔻Gently boosts immune defense (Wei Qi)

Avoid or use with caution if you have:
❌ Heat-type cough (yellow phlegm, sore throat, fever)
❌ Night sweats or yin deficiency
❌ Pregnancy (limit apricot kernels)
❌ Signs of internal heat (acne, thirst, irritability)

🍵 How to Make It

Ingredients:
• 6-8 green onion whites
• 1 small piece dried tangerine peel (chen pi)

3️⃣ Drink warm, add honey for taste

post_owner.name: Dr. Jenelle Kim
text:
The first thing I do in a hotel isn’t unpack.

I check the temperature.

In Eastern Medicine, cold is not neutral — especially when you’re traveling, run down, or trying to stay regulated. 
Cold can tighten the body, slow circulation, and make digestion and sleep feel “off” faster than you’d expect.

So before I settle in, I warm the space up and protect my system:

Raise the thermostat (or turn off blasting AC)

Take a warm shower to reset circulation

Keep my feet warm (yes, even in a “nice” hotel)

Order something warm first, not iced

It’s a small decision that keeps my energy steady… and my body feeling like it can actually rest.

O Menino do Poré que transformou a comunicação do RN. 📡

Milton Marques de Medeiros não foi apenas empresário. Foi médico, educador e visionário.

Natural de Upanema, sempre presente na comunidade do Poré (zona rural de Mossoró), carregou esse apelido com orgulho por toda a vida.

Sócio fundador da Rádio Princesa do Vale (região do Açú) e acionista da Rede Tropical de Comunicação, Milton enxergou o que poucos viam: a necessidade de uma comunicação local que realmente servisse o povo.

Em 2002, criou o maior conglomerado de comunicação do interior do Rio Grande do Norte: a TV Cabo Mossoró (TCM).

Hoje, o Grupo TCM de Comunicação reúne: 📡 Provedor de internet
📺 TV por assinatura e canal próprio
📻 Rede TCM de rádios
🎬 Produtora audiovisual TCP

Milton recebeu reconhecimento nacional pela criatividade e responsabilidade social.

Seu legado?

Vai muito além da estrutura empresarial. Está na visão de que comunicação local é ferramenta de transformação social.

O Menino do Poré se foi, mas sua trajetória permanece eternizada através do Grupo TCM, que continua honrando o compromisso de servir Mossoró e o Rio Grande do Norte.

⁠

⁠

What happens when we don’t process them is.

Emotions are energy in motion. They’re meant to be felt, moved through, and released - not suppressed, rushed, or ignored. When that doesn’t happen, they don’t disappear. They get stored in the body.

Here’s what most people don’t realize: your nervous system runs everything. Immunity, hormones, digestion, circulation, cardiovascular health, healing, regeneration, and emotional processing all depend on it.

When the nervous system becomes dysregulated, the body shifts into fight or flight. Survival mode. Resources are pulled away from healing and repair and redirected toward staying alive. In this state, balance, regeneration, and trauma processing are put on hold.

Unprocessed trauma doesn’t just live in the mind. It acts like a glitch in the body’s wiring. Signals misfire. Chemistry shifts. The body stays stuck in protection. This is why mindset work alone often isn’t enough to heal chronic symptoms.

One of the most powerful things we can do is support the parasympathetic nervous system - the rest, digest, and heal state. When the body feels safe, it can finally release stored emotions, regulate hormones, repair tissue, and move out of survival. It also allows the nervous system to shift smoothly between stress and rest instead of getting stuck.

When energy can’t move downward properly, it goes upward instead, leading to constipation along with burping, hiccups, nausea, acid reflux, bad breath, irritability, or ribcage tightness.

This is common postpartum and in older adults.

You may feel cold often, especially in your lower back or abdomen.

text:
Did you know that your emotions are linked to your organs?
 - and most people are missing this connection, definitely doctors are.

Emotions and our thoughts behind feelings affect our body more than most realize.
This connection is powerful, biological, and often overlooked.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, each organ is linked to a specific emotional pattern.

When an emotion becomes chronic or suppressed, it can weaken that organ over time.

Here’s the organ–emotion map:

→ guilt can weaken the heart
→ low self-esteem can weaken the pancreas
→ being controlling can affect the large intestine
→ being judgmental can weaken the small intestine
→ anger weakens the liver
→ bitterness weakens the gallbladder
→ chronic worry weakens the spleen
→ humiliation can affect the thyroid
→ being demanding weakens the stomach
→ feeling unsafe or vulnerable affects the skin
→ grief weakens the lungs
→ fear weakens the kidneys

Emotions themselves are not “bad.”
They are a normal and healthy part of being human.

The problem begins when emotions become intense, unresolved, or stuck.
This is when they can open the door to dis-ease.

TCM teaches that emotions are the main internal cause of illness,
but also one of the most changeable factors in healing.

Cause and effect are circular, not linear.
An emotion can weaken an organ → a weakened organ can intensify that same emotion.

The weaker the organ system, the more likely the emotional pattern appears.
The stronger the emotional pattern, the more the organ struggles.

This loop is why many people:
• eat well
• supplement
• detox
• “do all the right things”

…and still don’t fully heal.

The emotional body is often the missing piece.

If you’ve tried everything and still feel stuck, stored or trapped emotions may be worth addressing.

Modern research now supports this mind-body connection

text:
That anxiety feeling you experience during prep isn’t uncommon.

You’re down weight. The mirror is showing change. The information tracked confirms you’re trending in the right direction. But instead of feeling confident, you’re scanning for problems, you’re wondering if you should adjust macros, increase cardio, or change something JUST BECAUSE. 

This is prep anxiety, and it’s one of the most common psychological patterns I see in competitive athletes.

Here’s what’s actually happening: as you get leaner and closer to stage, the outside stress factors feel higher. Every day matters more. Your brain interprets this urgency as a signal that something must be wrong, even when the data says otherwise. You start looking for issues that don’t exist, requesting changes that aren’t needed, and second guessing a process that’s already working.

The truth? Anxiety doesn’t mean your prep is off track. It means you care.

But acting on that anxiety and making unnecessary adjustments, overcomplicating your protocol, or chasing perfection that isn’t there, can derail the very progress you’ve worked so hard to build.

This is why having a coach who can read the you in these moments AND manage the mental game is critical. Someone who knows when to adjust and when to stay the course. Someone who won’t react to your fear, but will respond to your physiology.

Progress isn’t always linear. But trust is. If the process is working, let it work. Your job isn’t to find problems. It’s to stay consistent, trust the plan, and show up every day, especially when your mind is telling you to panic.

That’s how a successful prep is built.

Later generations crossed the sea, settled elsewhere, and brought the oil with them, almost without realising it.

As Chinese migrants built lives across Southeast Asia, a small tin of Yu Yee Oil became part of the house. It came out for stomach aches, colds, insect bites, small burns. But it was never only about fixing something. It was about familiarity. A smell, a habit, a form of care that made new places feel a little more like home.

Every Asian mom says the same thing: never leave your hair wet — especially the roots! 🙅🏻‍♀️
And it’s not just an old wives’ tale.

From an Eastern medicine perspective, the head and neck are considered the body’s most vulnerable gateways. When the scalp is damp and exposed to cold air, circulation slows, cold “invades,” and the body’s natural defenses weaken first in this area — where colds, sinus issues, and headaches tend to start.

Western science explains the same phenomenon in a similar way: wet hair increases heat loss through evaporation. The scalp is highly vascular, so cold air exposure to wet hair pulls heat away quickly, lowering local & core temperature and triggering vasoconstriction. This reduces your immune activity, making you more susceptible to catching a cold & getting sick if you’re exposed to a virus or already in a less resilient state. 

So even if you’re in a rush or feeling lazy, just pull out that hair dryer so you don’t get sick!

Moms know best 🩵

text:
During my third trimester, birth was constantly on my mind.

At my 35-week ultrasound, they told me my baby was almost 6 pounds already. And someone said “Your baby will grow one pound a week past 37 weeks!” It freaked me out.

I’m not a big person. I was born at 6 pounds myself. And in my head, a “big baby” meant a hard birth. (Which is NOT true)

As a Chinese medicine practitioner, I’ve treated so many patients before and after births. I’ve treated people who were induced, people who had difficult labors, people who wished things went differently. 

I knew that birth is out of your control (so much so that I didn’t even want to write a birth plan, because you can’t “plan” anything. I still did eventually.) 

But I also knew that some of a smooth birth starts long before the actual labor begins.

So throughout my pregnancy after the first trimester ends, I stayed active. Prenatal yoga. Prenatal pilate. Swim. Chiropractic care. Acupuncture. Pelvic PT.

And still, when I was told my baby was bigger than expected, the anxiety crept in.

Then my yoga therapist @somayogaalx told me something that stayed with me, “Your body cannot grow a baby it cannot give birth to.” That really helped.

I know a lot of you are trying to get pregnant, who are pregnant. So I figured sharing what helped me have a smooth labor is a good idea.

If you’re feeling worried about birth, I want you to know you’re not alone. There are ways to support your body, calm your nervous system, and feel more grounded as you prepare.

Swipe to see the things that helped me support a smoother birth.

And also, remember that at the end of the day, one day, this chapter will pass. You’ll look at your baby and remembered how sweet the whole thing was.

You’ve got this! ❤️

It’s Dry January, let’s talk about it! In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), alcohol is generally discouraged, especially for those trying to conceive or improve overall health. With the recent study coming out about C and the risks of alcohol,here’s why TCM views alcohol as problematic:

1. Heat and Dampness
Alcohol is considered a heating substance in TCM, meaning it can create excessive internal heat, which disrupts the balance of Yin and Yang. It also generates dampness, a pathological condition associated with sluggishness, bloating, and accumulation of toxins in the body. Excessive heat and dampness can affect the liver, spleen, and reproductive system, which are crucial for fertility and overall vitality.

2. Liver Qi Stagnation
The liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and blood in TCM. Alcohol can overburden the liver, leading to Liver Qi stagnation. This stagnation can manifest as irritability, hormonal imbalances, or irregular menstrual cycles, all of which negatively impact fertility and overall health.

3. Weakened Kidney Essence
The kidneys are the foundation of reproductive health in TCM. Alcohol is thought to deplete Kidney Jing (Essence), the vital energy responsible for growth, reproduction, and aging. Depleting this energy can reduce fertility potential and weaken overall vitality.

4. Disturbs Shen (Spirit)
Excessive alcohol consumption is said to disturb the Shen, or spirit, leading to emotional instability, poor sleep, and mental fog. A calm Shen is essential for creating an optimal environment for conception and maintaining balance in daily life.
•
Alcohol in moderation may not harm everyone, but for those focused on fertility or holistic health, it can disrupt energy flow, weaken vital organs, and hinder balance. In TCM, abstaining or greatly reducing alcohol is often recommended to maintain harmony and health.

text:
Two weeks ago, I made sweet rice wine in a traditional fermentation jar.
The rice settled.
The liquid clarified.
A young wine began to form.

My original plan was to store it —
to let it mature quietly over time.

But studying the foundations of Chinese medicine has been teaching me to notice when something is ready to continue, rather than simply be preserved.

To guide sweet rice wine toward vinegar, the method is simple — but precise.

The alcohol is lowered with clean water.
The vessel is opened and widened.
The surface is exposed to air.
Nothing is sealed.

Wine is made without oxygen.
Vinegar only exists because of it.

In Chinese medicine, both have their place.

Rice wine is warming and dispersing.
It moves and opens.
Traditionally, it’s used as a medium —
to carry, to activate, and to guide substances in cooking, fermentation, and external preparations.

Vinegar works differently.

It gathers.
It tightens.
It draws inward.

Vinegar has long been used to harmonize movement, soften accumulation, and act as a solvent —
in cooking, fermentation, and topical or external applications —
where direction and containment are needed rather than force.

What was once sweet doesn’t disappear.
It transforms.

It tightens.
It becomes sour.

It’s winter now — the Water phase — a season that teaches descent, storage, and quiet change beneath the surface.

Maclee Materia lives in this relationship:
between old and new,
between study and practice,
between allowing and guiding.

text:
Dein Ventil muss sich irgendwo entleeren. Kopfschmerzen gelten in der TCM oft als Überhitzung 🔥
 
Das ist meine persönliche 1️⃣ Wahrheit. 

2️⃣ Wahrheit lautet: Die Faszien auf der Kopfhaut werden mit jeden Gedanken immer straffer. Der Kopf hat zu wenig Platz & will sich Platz durch Druck verschaffen. Doch die Faszien ziehen sich immer weiter wie ein Netz zusammen. 

Die persönliche 3️⃣ Wahrheit von mir: Deine Gedanken wollen gehört werden, doch du drückst sie weg. Bis das Ventil platzt & dieses Hitzegefühl im Kopf wieder da ist. 

Punkt 4️⃣: Deine Faszien wollen die unterdrückten Gedanken nicht mehr in deinem Körper tragen. Faszien haben unter anderem die Aufgabe für Halt & Stabilität zu sorgen. Doch zu viel Halt, lässt deine Faszien starr werden. Hier kommt es darauf an, wie viel Raum du deinen Faszien & Gedanken gibst damit sie wieder geschmeidig werden & fließen können. 

Und zum Abschluss meine persönliche 5️⃣ Wahrheit: Laut der TCM ist jedes Körpersymptom einem Ungleichgewicht zwischen den Energien Yin und Yang zurückzuführen. Kopfschmerzen haben oft zu viel Yang (der Blasenmeridian verläuft genau übern Kopf und gehört dem Yang an - typisch für dieses "Hitze-" und "Stauungsgefühl"). Yang ist die männliche Energie. Das Durchhalten. Immer nur zu funktionieren. Und das Vergessen auf die körpereigene Intuition. Die Harmonie & Balance was das Yin, die weibliche sanfte Energie mit sich bringt. Dein aktives Yang unterdrückt dein sanftes Yin. Doch beide Energien wollen im Gleichgewicht  bleiben, damit der Körper & Geist in Balance leben kann. 

Welche persönliche Wahrheit trifft auf dich zu? Schreib mir gern eine Zahl von 1-5 in den Kommentaren 👇🏻

Much love
Patrizia

❤️Ginseng Chicken Tonic for Fatigue and Stress

If you’ve been feeling tired but wired and never well rested, burnt out, dry inside from winter heating, or just running on empty, this is one of the most supportive TCM soups you can make. This is a gentle tonic that restores Qi and Yin at the same time while calming internal heat and supporting digestion. Perfect for:

✨ burnout & overworking
✨ dry throat or dry cough
✨ “tired but wired” stress
✨ mild deficiency heat
✨ winter dryness from indoor heating
✨ recovery after illness
✨ postpartum week 3–4 (after heat clears)

It’s clear, slightly sweet, gently cooling-but-nourishing — the kind of quiet, steady support your body feels immediately.

Ingredients:
🍗 5-6 fresh chicken drumsticks – strengthen Spleen Qi for steady energy
🌿 1-2 fresh American/Canadian ginseng (花旗参) – nourishes Yin, cools deficiency heat, supports mental clarity
🐚 10 dried scallops (乾瑤柱) – deepen the umami and strengthen Spleen + Kidney
❤️ 10 dried red dates (紅棗) – nourish Blood, harmonize the formula
🍇 10 dried red goji berries (枸杞) – moisten dryness + support Liver/Kidney Yin
🤍 Fresh Chinese yam (淮山)– tonifies Qi + Yin and supports digestion
💧 2 L of water

In your pot (I’m using a ceramic pot), you can panfry the chicken drumsticks to brown them for more flavour. Once that’s browned, add in 2L of water and bring that to a boil. Once that boils, add in your American ginseng, scallops, goji berries, red dates, and Chinese yam and boil covered for another 2 hours on medium heat (gentle bubbling). Salt gently to taste.

⚠️ Who Should Avoid This Soup?

Because American ginseng is cooling, skip this soup if you have:
• cold hands/feet or loose stools
• Spleen/Kidney Yang deficiency
• active cold/flu symptoms
• dampness or phlegm
• very weak digestion

🌸You can find the full recipe here: https://thechinesesouplady.com/ginseng-chicken-tonic-for-fatigue-and-stress/

This technique is actually a legitimate qigong practice for circulation and energy flow - but let's be clear about what it actually does and doesn't do.

What you're seeing here is a specific tapping sequence targeting meridian endpoints in traditional Chinese medicine. The cupping motion creates vibration that practitioners believe stimulates energy channels connected to the heart and upper body.

In TCM theory, your hands contain the endpoints of major meridians - Pericardium, Heart, Lung, Large Intestine, Small Intestine, and Triple Burner channels. Tapping these areas is meant to promote qi flow, reduce stagnation, and support overall circulation.

The number nine has significance in many traditional practices - it's considered a completion number, representing fullness and cycles. The cupping technique rather than flat palm creates deeper vibration into tissues without causing pain or surface trauma.

Here's what this practice can actually do: improve circulation, reduce tension, support relaxation, potentially lower stress hormones, and create a meditative focus. Many people report feeling more energized and less tense after regular practice.

Here's what it cannot do: clear arterial plaque, replace cardiac medication, treat diagnosed heart disease, or substitute for medical intervention when needed.

Think of it like stretching or massage - beneficial for overall wellness, circulation support, and stress reduction. Not a replacement for medical care when there's actual pathology.

If you have heart concerns, see a cardiologist. Practice this as complementary wellness, not alternative medicine.

text:
Let’s talk about dry January! In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), alcohol is generally discouraged, especially for those trying to conceive or improve overall health. With the recent study coming out about C and the risks of alcohol,here’s why TCM views alcohol as problematic:

1. Heat and Dampness
Alcohol is considered a heating substance in TCM, meaning it can create excessive internal heat, which disrupts the balance of Yin and Yang. It also generates dampness, a pathological condition associated with sluggishness, bloating, and accumulation of toxins in the body. Excessive heat and dampness can affect the liver, spleen, and reproductive system, which are crucial for fertility and overall vitality.

2. Liver Qi Stagnation
The liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and blood in TCM. Alcohol can overburden the liver, leading to Liver Qi stagnation. This stagnation can manifest as irritability, hormonal imbalances, or irregular menstrual cycles, all of which negatively impact fertility and overall health.

3. Weakened Kidney Essence
The kidneys are the foundation of reproductive health in TCM. Alcohol is thought to deplete Kidney Jing (Essence), the vital energy responsible for growth, reproduction, and aging. Depleting this energy can reduce fertility potential and weaken overall vitality.

4. Disturbs Shen (Spirit)
Excessive alcohol consumption is said to disturb the Shen, or spirit, leading to emotional instability, poor sleep, and mental fog. A calm Shen is essential for creating an optimal environment for conception and maintaining balance in daily life.
•
Alcohol in moderation may not harm everyone, but for those focused on fertility or holistic health, it can disrupt energy flow, weaken vital organs, and hinder balance. In TCM, abstaining or greatly reducing alcohol is often recommended to maintain harmony and health.

Na Medicina Tradicional Chinesa, a temperatura da água é tão importante quanto a quantidade.

Líquidos muito frios tendem a enfraquecer o Baço e o Estômago, que são responsáveis pela digestão, pela transformação dos alimentos e pela produção de energia.

A água morna facilita esse processo.
Ela preserva o calor interno, ajuda o Qi a circular, favorece a circulação do Sangue e apoia a digestão sem sobrecarregar o organismo.

Por isso, aquecer a água é especialmente benéfica para:
• mulheres mais sensíveis ao frio 🥶 
• quem sente mãos e pés frios 🧦🧤
• fadiga com sensação de peso 🥱
• retenção de líquidos 🥴
• digestão lenta e inchaço abdominal🤰🏻

🩸CÓLICAS : para que tem cólicas que pioram com frio ( e melhoram com calor: bolsa quente, banho quente) também vão se beneficiar com a água quente/morna 🫶 já que vai aquecer o baixo ventre, favorecer a circulação do Sangue, reduzir a contração causada pelo frio, assim diminuir a intensidade do desconforto. 

✨ E o que a ciência observa:
líquidos em temperatura morna tendem a ser melhor tolerados pelo sistema digestivo, exigindo menos ajustes térmicos do corpo e favorecendo o esvaziamento gástrico.

Você pode começar temperando a água temperatura ambiente com morna e ir aquecendo aos poucos. Leve sua garrafinha térmica e me conte depois se não se sente melhor 🥰

🍊✨ Salted Steamed Orange — A TCM Home Remedy

If you grew up in a Chinese household, you probably know this one: salted steamed orange for cough, light phlegm, and scratchy throats. It’s simple, comforting, and surprisingly effective from a TCM perspective.

🌿 TCM Benefits of Salted Steamed Orange:
🍊 Transforms light phlegm, moistens the lungs, soften sticky mucus, soothe dryness in the lungs
🧂 Salt has an anchoring, directing effect. It regulates Lung Qi, softens phlegm, draws fluids downward
🍊 Relieves dry or lingering cough, throat itchiness, nighttime cough
🍊 Warming without overheating, which is also great for kids! It supports digestion, gently moves Qi, warms the middle

🍵 How to Make It (Simple!)
	1. Wash one orange
	2. Cut off the top
	3. Sprinkle a pinch of salt inside
	4. Steam for 10–15 minutes
	5. Eat the warm fruit + drink the juice

That’s it — a nostalgic, effective TCM home remedy you can make anytime.

⚠️ Who Should Avoid? Skip or reduce salt if you have:
🍊 high blood pressure
🍊 heavy phlegm-heat (very yellow mucus, fever)
🍊 active sore throat with heat signs

For phlegm-heat, go toward pear, chrysanthemum, honeysuckle, or mung bean teas instead.

Modern nutrition calls it vitamin C + warm hydration.

Here's the paradox for Eastern Medicine practitioners:

We know we need to grow and develop skills, yet we tend to only focus on one type.

Yes our clinical skills will always keep developing. But for most of us the weakest link in the chain has nothing to do with technical knowledge of the medicine.

To identify the weakest link we first need to understand the chain. 

The anatomy of a healthy business includes:

1. Attraction (the ability to generate interest in your work)
2. Conversion (educating potential patients on the unique truths of your practice)
3. Sales (the ability to create strong working relationships through offers that make sense and feel right to you and the people you're working with)
4. Product (the delivery of services like acupuncture, herbs, lifestyle advice etc)

"Opportunity cost" refers to losing the potential benefits of option B by choosing option A.

In our case most practitioners double or triple down on building up skill 4 by attending more and more technical seminars rather than building skills in 1-3.

Yes it's fun to learn new clinical pearls. But I had to realize that in order to better serve, I had to develop skills 1-3.

text:
🌸 Canadian (American) Ginseng in Teas & Soups

If you’ve ever felt tired but hot, burnt out but wired, or dry inside from stress or winter heating, Canadian/American ginseng (花旗参) is one of the most beautiful tonic herbs to turn to. 💛

This ginseng is cooling in nature and nourishes Qi + Yin at the same time. It builds energy, calms internal heat, and supports the Heart, Lungs, and Kidneys — all without being too stimulating or warming.

🌸 1. Build Qi + Energy (Soup)
Fresh or 5-6 slices dried ginseng + 10 dried scallops + 1 whole chicken + 10 red dates + fresh Chinese yam + 2.5L 
For burnout, weak digestion, long-term fatigue, overwork. This is a gentle recovery soup that nourishes Qi without overheating.

🌸 2. Cool Mild Heat + Calm the Mind (Tea)
3-4 slices dried ginseng + 10 chrysanthemum baby buds + honey to taste + 1 cup of boiling water
For irritability, tension headaches, dry eyes, stress heat. Perfect for people who feel mentally tired but “hot” inside.

🌸 3. Moisten Dryness + Soothe the Throat (Tea)
3-4 slices dried ginseng + 7 dried goji berries (or 5 dried mulberries) + honey + 1 cup of boiling water
For dry cough, dry throat, heated indoor climates, winter dryness. A beautiful Lung Yin–nourishing tea.

🌸 4. Post-Recovery + Kidney Support (Soup)
5–6 slices dried ginseng + fish (any type) + 1–2 slices fresh ginger + red dates + fresh Chinese yam (optional)
For postpartum week 3–4, recovery after illness, exhaustion with dryness. A clean, restorative tonic that will help rebuild Qi gently into the more stable postpartum recovery moments.

⚠️ Avoid if:
• cold constitution (cold hands/feet, loose stools, low appetite)
• yang deficiency (Spleen/Kidney cold, bloating after cold foods)
• active cold or wind-cold illness (chills, early cold symptoms)
• dampness or phlegm (heaviness, sticky tongue coat, congestion)
• very weak digestion (easily bloated, sluggish after meals)

Think of it as a calm, steady recharge, rather than a stimulating boost.

Bij blaasontsteking (branderig plassen, veel aandrang, druk in de onderbuik) ziet de Traditionele Chinese Geneeskunde vaak Damp-Hitte en stagnatie in de Blaasmeridiaan.

Een belangrijk ondersteunend punt hierbij is BL-60 (Kūnlún).

📍 BL-60

Achter de enkel, in de kuil tussen de buitenste enkelknobbel en de achillespees.

Dit punt helpt om:
✔️ hitte te klaren
✔️ spanning te laten zakken
✔️ de Blaasmeridiaan te laten stromen

👣 Waarom masseren van BL-67 → BL-60?

De Blaasmeridiaan loopt tot aan de kleine teen (BL-67).
Door van BL-67 richting BL-60 te masseren:

	•	volg je de natuurlijke stroom van Qi
	•	help je hitte en druk af te voeren
	•	kan aandrang en branderigheid verminderen

✋ Zo doe je het

1–2× per dag:
• Start bij BL-67 (buitenhoek kleine teen)
• Volg de buitenrand van de voet omhoog
• Eindig met rustige, diepe druk op BL-60 (1–2 min)

In de Chinese geneeskunde wordt “compost” gezien als een belangrijke oorzaak van ziekten. Compost heeft de neiging om de functies van het lichaam te belemmeren en zoekt altijd een weg naar buiten, weg van belangrijke organen. 
Overgewicht, acne, eczeem, lipoedeem, chronische verkoudheid ea zijn duidelijke symptomen van compost.
Compost (overmatig vocht) onstaat als voedsel niet goed omgezet kan worden in voedingsstoffen.
Compost is geen vocht in de letterlijke zin, maar is plakkerig en troebel. Je kunt het vergelijken met mist of modder.

Meestal willen we op een ongezonde manier compost aanpakken: als we puistjes hebben geven we aandacht aan het gezicht, haaruitval krijgt een andere shampoo, overgewicht krijgt minder calorieën, eczeem krijgt een zalfje, een aanhoudende verkoudheid een pilletje.
Helaas kunnen we ons lichaam niet lang voor de gek houden en door medicatie of diëten stapelt compost zich nog sneller op. We zijn na een dieet misschien gewicht verloren maar de oorzaak (compost) is niet aangekeken. Compost + de verloren kilo's komen terug en klachten stapelen zich op.

Verkeerde, te weinig of teveel voeding kunnen het lichaam ziek maken. Ook angst, pessimisme, stress en gedachten hebben invloed. Tijdens een consult breng ik in beeld hoe jouw lichaam het beste compost kan oplossen en hoe je een opstapeling kunt voorkomen.

❤️ Let’s talk ginseng! 

Today’s spotlight is on American / Canadian ginseng (西洋参 xi yang shen, but sometimes also called 人参 ren shen) — a completely different herb from Korean (red) ginseng. Same family, totally different temperatures in TCM.

If you’ve ever felt confused about which ginseng to buy… this one’s for you. 💛

🌿 What American/Canadian Ginseng Actually Does (TCM View)

This type of ginseng is cooling, moistening, and calming. It supports the Lung, Heart, and Kidney systems, and builds Qi + Yin gently — without overstimulating the body.

Think of it like this:
🌸 American/Canadian ginseng = fixing the air-conditioning system (cooling, moistening, and replenishes yin)
🌸 Korean ginseng = heating the body’s furnace (warms the body and boosts yang.)

If you feel warm because your “cooling system” is broken (Yin deficiency), this is the ginseng you want. Not for putting out fires, but for rebuilding internal fluids.

🌸 Best For (Yin Deficiency Signs): Afternoon fatigue with warmth, night heat / night sweats, low-grade fevers, irritability from exhaustion, shortness of breath, dryness (skin, mouth, throat), feeling tired from long hours or poor sleep

🍵 How I Use It

My favourite everyday tonic:
✨ 3–5 slices in hot water
✨ Add a little honey
✨ Sip and refill throughout the day
✨ I also use them in soups, which make amazing tonics!

⚠️ Avoid American/Canadian Ginseng if you have an active cold or flu, fever or infection, loose stools or bloating, heavy dampness in the body (too cooling + too moistening for these patterns.)

American/Canadian ginseng is a short-term, food-grade tonic — perfect for those moments when you feel dry, tired, and worn down, but not something to take every single day forever (unless otherwise advised by a TCM, please do check!). I always bring dried ginseng when traveling. It’s easy, gentle, and incredibly supportive when your system needs a reset.

🌸What to Address First in TCM?🌸

🌸 Full explanation video for subscribers. 

When your body is giving you multiple symptoms at the same time, on top of the weather, how do you know what to support first? In TCM, there is a very simple logic that keeps things clear and avoids making imbalances worse.

1️⃣ Root or Branch?

Root = underlying cause
Branch = symptoms happening right now

✨ If symptoms are severe → treat the branch first.
Think: fever, swelling, infection, acute cough, sharp pain. These need cooling or clearing foods/teas right away.

✨ If symptoms are mild + chronic → treat the root. Think: fatigue, weak digestion, cold limbs, poor sleep.
This is where slow, nourishing soups work best.

2️⃣ Is it EXCESS or DEFICIENCY? This is the key question in TCM.

⭐ First priority: Clear excess. 
👉 Removing the “blockage” first creates space for the body to heal. There are exceptions though, such as when the body is too weak to eliminate the pathogens. 
⭐ After excess is cleared → gently tonify.

When you nourish at the right time, the body absorbs it better.

3️⃣ Adapt to season, diet, and taste.

Your diet should shift with the environment around you.

⭐This is the foundation of choosing the right soups, teas, and ingredients at the right time at the right moment. Remember, symptoms shift as well… even though it could be the same condition.

SP-10 ligt net boven de knieschijf, aan de binnenzijde van het bovenbeen, als je recht omhoog gaat langs de binnenkant van de knieschijf in een zachte kuil op de spier. Het punt hoort bij de Milt-meridiaan, die in TCM een grote rol speelt in bloed, voeding en huid.

🌼 TCM Tea for Mouth Ulcers & Cold Sores 🌼

This is my gentle go-to soothing tea for painful mouth ulcers, cold sores, inflamed gums, or a severe sore throats. I often develop this after a lot of hot pot, Korean bbq, or eating a lot of fried foods and poor sleep.

In TCM, mouth sores are often a sign of excess heat — commonly heart heat, stomach heat, or toxic heat flaring upward. Instead of suppressing symptoms, this tea works by clearing heat, soothing inflammation, and protecting the throat and mouth lining.

🍵 What’s in this tea & why it works

🌼 Chrysanthemum buds (菊花) - use 10 baby buds
• Clears wind-heat, reduces inflammation in the mouth & throat, calms irritation and redness

🌿 Honeysuckle (金银花) - use 1 teaspoon
• Clears toxic heat, excellent for sores, swelling, and infections, helps shorten healing time

🌱 Licorice Root (甘草) - 1-2 slices (it’s got a unique slightly bitter taste)
• A neutral root that soothes pain and irritation, protects the mouth and throat lining, harmonizes the formula and calms spasms

🍯 Honey (added after boiling) - taste as needed
• Moistens dryness, coats ulcers gently, helps reduce pain and irritation

🫖I boiled the herbs for 8-10 minutes on the stove, let it cool slightly before adding honey. Drink warm, 1–2 cups per day during flare-ups.

🔥 Who this tea is good for

🔻 Mouth ulcers or canker sores, cold sores inside the mouth
🔻 Gum inflammation or sore throat with heat signs
🔻 Stress-related flare-ups, poor sleep, or overwork triggering sores

⚠️ Not ideal if you have chills, watery mucus, or a cold-type sore throat.

🌿 TCM tip

Recurring mouth sores are often a sign the body needs more rest, better stress regulation, less spicy, fried, or alcohol-based foods. Cooling teas help — but addressing the root matters most!

Because then they'll be able to have it every day.

Because here's a thought experiment:

What is the highest value use of your time?

For an acupuncturist it's going to be - guess what - doing acupuncture!

Yes cupping is great. Yes gua sha is great. Yes massage is great. Yes moxa is great.

Maclee Materia — Episode 1, Part 1
Sweet Rice Wine (Jiǔ Niáng 酒酿)

This is where my Traditional Chinese Medicine kitchen cabinet begins.
With Rice.

As Metal season closes and we enter Water, the work turns inward. We turn inward. 
What we store now becomes what carries us forward.

My method:
Wash short-grain rice until the water runs clear.
Soak, then steam until fully cooked.
Let the rice cool completely.
Crush Chinese yeast balls into a fine powder and massage evenly into the rice.
Transfer to a clean fermentation jar.
Add a small portion of last year’s sweet rice wine to seed the batch.
Cover and ferment in a dark, warm place.

Timing:
Sweetness appears in about 3–5 days.
Sweet rice wine forms in 2–4 weeks.
With time — months to a year — it deepens into a mature mother batch
(usually around 10–15% alcohol).

In Traditional Chinese medicine, rice is Gu Qi — the steady nourishment that supports all transformation.
Through fermentation, rice becomes sweet rice wine: warming, harmonizing, and connective.

In my Maclee Materia cabinet, this wine moves forward into cooking as food-medicine, warming the middle, seasonal dishes, and topical ritual craft.

This is a yearly practice.
Old feeding new.
Respecting the past to create what comes next.

Love, Maclee

text:
Budzisz się między pierwszą a trzecią w nocy? Znasz to uczucie, prawda? Serce przyspiesza, myśli wirują, a sen odpływa.

Starożytni chińscy lekarze zauważyli coś fascynującego: w tych godzinach wątroba pracuje na najwyższych obrotach. Nie tylko oczyszcza krew, ale według TCM przetwarza też emocje – ten gniew, który przełknąłeś w pracy, lęk, o którym nie chcesz mówić, rozczarowania, które starannie chowasz.

I wiesz co? Nauka to potwierdza, tylko innymi słowami. Badacze odkryli, że wątroba ma swój wewnętrzny zegar biologiczny osiągający szczyt aktywności właśnie w nocy (PMID: 31711683). Każda komórka wątroby ma molekularny mechanizm odmierzający czas w rytmie 24-godzinnym.

Ale jest więcej. Naukowcy z UC Berkeley pokazali, że podczas snu w fazie REM nasz mózg przepracowuje emocjonalne wspomnienia. Amygdala - odpowiedzialna za strachy - przechodzi przez nocną terapię, reorganizując i zmniejszając emocjonalny ładunek wspomnień (PMID: 22119526).

Problem? Chroniczny stres. Kortyzol, który normalnie delikatnie wzrasta o 2-3 w nocy, u przemęczonych osób wystrzeliwuje jak rakieta. Aktywuje układ współczulny; serce przyspiesza, ciało przechodzi w tryb "walcz lub uciekaj". I właśnie wtedy się budzisz (PMID: 20628523).

Widzisz wzór? Starożytna wiedza spotyka się z neuroscience i chronobiologią.

Co możesz zrobić? Regularne godziny snu to podstawa – zegar biologiczny kocha przewidywalność. Lekka kolacja 3-4h przed snem. Więcej warzyw krzyżowych (brokuły, kalafior) wspierających detoksyfikację wątroby. Wieczorny journaling – wypuść na papier to, co leży na sercu. Magnez przed snem, techniki oddechowe, ashwagandha dla kortyzolu.

Ale uwaga: Jeśli budzisz się regularnie, nie ignoruj tego. Może to być objaw bezdechów, problemów z tarczycą, refluksu czy lęku. Medycyna integracyjna to "razem z", nie "zamiast". Wizyta u specjalisty to zawsze dobry pierwszy krok.

Twoje ciało próbuje z tobą rozmawiać. Czasem najlepsze, co możesz zrobić, to zacząć słuchać. 💚

post_owner.name: Jeremy Cornish
text:
When Eastern Medicine Practitioners expand into offering online programs, one of the common questions that comes up is "what do I do about the pulse?" 
 
I'll give you 3 ways to take the pulse online. But first... 
 
It may be worthwhile to examine why we feel we need to take the pulse in the first place. 
 
Of course there are some system that are heavily reliant on pulse characteristics in order to pick an herbal formula. 
 
And if that's something you're using in clinic successfully, don't change it. 
 
What we can do instead is start thinking a little differently for our online folks. It doesn't cost anything to expand our beliefs. Maybe there are other sources of information we can use to choose herbs without having access to a pulse at all? 
 
A quick search of @tcmweaver (see slides) shows there are 365 herbal formulas that don't have any sort of pulse listed as an indication. So that clearly means there are other ways to pick a formula that don't all require taking pulse. 
 
That said: 
 
1. Information on the rate of the pulse can help us determine if there's cold or heat as part of the pattern. Can you ask someone to measure their pulse rate themselves and let you know what it is? 
2. The strength of the pulse can be helpful for determining excess or deficiency. Can you ask someone what their blood pressure is? Would that give you a good idea of excess and deficiency? 
3. Can you teach your patients to feel basic qualities of the pulse such as wiry, choppy, slippery? That could be valuable for them to learn more about themselves and helpful information for you as well. 
 
With a flexible and open mind we can find all sorts of creative solutions to practice in the modern age. 
 
And remembering to base our treatment on a constellation of relevant information (not just one data point) will make us better at seeing the larger picture

text:
Astronomisch begint de winter pas rond 21 december. Maar als ik eerlijk ben? Mijn lichaam zit er al weken in. En misschien herken je dat wel. De dagen zijn kort, het is koud, en als het aan je lichaam ligt wil je eigenlijk gewoon op de bank met een deken en thee. Maar in plaats daarvan... check je je to-do lijst, plan je kerstdiners, en probeer je nog even snel alles af te ronden. 

In de Iokai Shiatsu werken we met de vijf elementen. En deze tijd van het jaar hoort bij het water element. Water staat voor rust, stilte, naar binnen keren. Het seizoen van opslaan en herstellen. Denk aan hoe de natuur zich terugtrekt. Zaden die in de aarde rusten en kracht verzamelen. Dieren houden een winterslaap. Alles gaat op een lager pitje. En eigenlijk zou jouw lichaam dat ook willen doen. 

Maar wij blijven maar doorgaan.... 

We leven in een cultuur die geen seizoenen kent. Altijd dezelfde productiviteit, altijd “aan”. En je lichaam voelt dat. In shiatsu kijken we naar de nier- en blaasmeridianen die horen bij het water element. Als die uit balans zijn, merk je dat aan vermoeidheid die niet weggaat, onderrugklachten, koude handen en voeten, angst of onzekerheid of wilskracht die ontbreekt. 
Klinkt bekend? Dan vraagt je lichaam waarschijnlijk om wat meer aandacht voor die waterfase-energie. 

Winter is geen seizoen om door te worstelen. Het is een seizoen om te herstellen. Zodat je straks, als de energie weer omhoog gaat, klaar bent voor wat er komen gaat. Je lichaam weet echt wel wat het nodig heeft. Soms moeten we alleen even leren luisteren.

post_owner.name: Functional Fine Bone China 🌬
text:
It's so difficult to stay hydtated during the colder months! So here's a little 💨 Baddie Beauty Hack that's been used in traditional chinese medicine for probably thousands of years. ✨️

Snow fungus soup with apples and lotus seeds is a popular, nourishing Chinese dessert that is easy to make and can be served warm or chilled. It is believed to be beneficial for skin health, lung function, and general well-being. 

I used 3 medium snow fungus heads (soaked)

2 medium apples

 A hand full of white lotus seeds pre pitted. 

10 red dates (jujubes), pitted and chopped
A Hand full of Peach Gum (Soaked and cleaned)

8 cups (about 2 Liters) water, plus more for soaking

Rock sugar (to taste), cinnamon to taste,vanilla to taste

*A couple table spoons of chia seeds, you can also use basil seeds.

Instructions
Prepare the dried ingredients:

Soak the snow fungus in cold water for at least 30 minutes, or until it has fully expanded and turned soft. Trim and discard the hard, dark yellow base with kitchen scissors, then tear the rest into bite-sized pieces.

Rinse the lotus seeds & peach gum. Soak them seperately in warm water for about 30 minutes. 

Rinse the red dates, remove the pits and chop them. 

Prepare the apples:
Wash the apples thoroughly. You can peel them if you prefer, but it is not necessary. Core the apples and cut them into wedges or chunks. Soaking the cut apples in lightly salted water can prevent browning before cooking.

Cook the soup:
In a large pot, bring 8 cups of water to a boil. Add the prepared snow fungus, lotus seeds, and red dates, chia seeds. Stir occasionally so the chia seeds don't clump
 
Once the water boils again, reduce the heat to low, cover the pot with a lid (leaving a small vent), and simmer for at least 60-90 minutes, or until the snow fungus reaches your desired soft, gelatinous consistency.
Finish and serve:
During the final 5-10 minutes of simmering, add the apple chunks, cinnamon, vanilla extract and rock sugar to taste. Stir until the sugar is fully dissolved.

Serve and enjoy!

text:
The holiday season in Minnesota has a rhythm all its own. The early sunsets, the cold air, and the steady stream of celebrations can quietly burn through your Yin, the cooling, restorative reserve that keeps you grounded.

December naturally leans Yang: bright, busy, outward, fast. And when that outweighs the quieter moments, your Yin works overtime to keep things balanced. It’s easy to feel that reserve thinning with more stimulation, more commitments, and more late nights.

Supporting your Yin doesn’t require a full retreat. It’s about small, intentional pauses: a slow walk in the cold air, an early night once a week, warm and simple meals between rich gatherings, fewer stimulants when the season already feels loud, and the rituals that steady you: meditation, breathwork, or a few quiet minutes before the house wakes up.

Minnesota winters invite us inward for a reason. When you honor your Yin in these small ways, you move through the holidays with more steadiness, presence, and warmth, a season that feels good, not just full.

A TCM view: How much energy does it take your body to heat 1 cup of cold water?

Drinking one cup of ice water forces your body to burn ~8.8 kcal just to warm it to body temperature.
That’s NOT from fat loss — it’s your precious metabolic energy (Qi in TCM) being diverted from vital functions.

🔬 To heat 237 mL (1 cup) of 0°C water to 37°C:
Energy = 237g×4.184Jg°C×37°C ≈ 8.8 kcal Energy

🧠 42 minutes of brain metabolism
❤️ 880 heartbeats (12 minutes of heart work)
🫘 2 hours of kidney filtration
🔥 8.5 minutes of total body basal metabolism

Traditional Chinese Medicine has warned against cold drinks as “cold drinks injure the spleen and stomach.” The spleen yang provides digestive “fire” and cold water extinguishes this fire → body borrows yang Qi from other functions, resulting in poor digestion, dampness, weak immunity, mental clarity, slower blood circulation, lower immunity (wei qi).

Veel mensen noemen nachtelijk wakker worden “stress”.
Maar als je eerlijk bent, voelt het vaak anders: je bent doodmoe… en toch lig je ineens klaarwakker. Alsof je lichaam niet kan doorslapen, ook al wil jij dat wel.

In de Chinese geneeskunde kijken we niet alleen naar het symptoom “wakker worden”, maar naar het patroon erachter: wat zet jouw systeem ’s nachts aan?

Herken je dit?

Je valt prima in slaap, maar wordt een paar uur later wakker en komt moeilijk terug weg. Dit zien we vaak bij Yin-tekort: het lichaam heeft te weinig herstel-reserve om de slaap diep te houden.

Word je bijna elke nacht rond hetzelfde tijdstip wakker?
Dan gebruiken we de orgaanklok als aanwijzing. Tussen 01:00–03:00 ligt vaak de nadruk op Lever (spanning, piekeren, opgekropte emotie). Tussen 03:00–05:00 zien we vaker Longen (onrust, verdriet, “niet kunnen zakken”).

Word je wakker met warmte, spanning, hartkloppingen of druk in je hoofd?
Dat past bij een systeem dat te actief blijft in de nacht: vaak Yin is te laag of Yang gaat omhoog.

Slapen is geen trucje.
Als je ’s nachts wakker wordt, is dat meestal omdat je lichaam iets mist (herstel/voeding) óf omdat er te veel “aan” staat (spanning/activatie). En zolang je dat patroon niet herkent, blijf je dezelfde cirkel draaien.

Postpartum hair shedding isn’t a flaw, it’s a signal from your body. 

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the scalp and hair are supported by blood flow, warmth, nourishment, and nervous system safety. After birth, the body is rebuilding and gentle support matters.

TCM-inspired ways to support the scalp postpartum:

✨ Nourish from within
Warm meals, bone broth, eggs, leafy greens, black sesame, and mineral-rich foods help rebuild what the body used during pregnancy.

✨ Keep the body + scalp warm
Avoid cold drinks, cold air, and going outside with wet hair. Warmth supports circulation and hormonal balance.

✨ Gentle scalp care
Soft fingertip massage at the temples, crown, and nape encourages blood flow without stressing fragile follicles.

✨ Slow, mindful combing
Use a wooden or jade comb to gently brush from front to back. Calming the scalp and nervous system.

✨ Support the nervous system
Rest, deep breathing, and slowing down help signal safety to the body (and hair).

✨ Trust the timing
Postpartum shedding is temporary. When the body is supported and restored, regrowth follows.

When the root is nourished, the hair responds 🤍

👉 Jede Narbe kann den Fluss deiner Lebensenergie – des Qi – blockieren.

Narben liegen häufig direkt auf Meridianen, also auf den Energiebahnen deines Körpers.

🔹 Eine Blinddarmnarbe liegt auf dem Verdauungsmeridian.

Wenn dort Energie blockiert ist, kann sie nicht mehr frei fließen.

• Rückenschmerzen
• ständige Müdigkeit
• Verdauungsprobleme
• hormonelle Schwankungen
• Gelenk- oder Bewegungseinschränkungen

Narben sind nicht einfach Vergangenheit.
Sie können ein aktives Störfeld im Körper sein – auch nach Jahrzehnten.

dann kommentiere Erstgespräch unter diesem Reel.

text:
Ep. 8: Tired Eyes👀😵[read💌⤵️]

Don’t you feel tired from overscrolling all the time? Cuz I do～if you know you know... I’m Chee Hee, a Chinese Medicine student from Malaysia 🇲🇾 and I’m graduating this year! Before that, I want to take you on this journey with me and learn different acupuncture points in your body that you can massage yourself for specific conditions 💛 Join me and follow along for more.

In this episode, I introduced four acupuncture points that are commonly used together to relieve eye strain. In Chinese Medicine, acupressure can help with strained eyes by promoting circulation in related meridians, such as the liver, kidney, and spleen meridians. Research on the relationship between acupressure and eye health is minimal. However, it’s believed that massaging specific acupressure points may provide relief for certain acute and chronic eye conditions.

1️⃣Zanzhu (UB-2) Urinary Bladder Channel, lies in the depressions at the inner ends of the eyebrows.

2️⃣Yuyao: Midpoint of the eyebrow in the hollow. Good for eye problems related to worry, excessive study and mental strain.

3️⃣Taiyang: In the region of the temples, in the depression about one finger-breadth posterior to the midpoint between the lateral end of the eyebrow and the outer canthus.

4️⃣Chengqi: With the eyes looking straight forward, the acupoint is directly below the pupil, between the eyeball and the lower eye socket bone ridge.

Massage gently in small circles for 1-3 minutes. You should have a deep aching feeling on the point and a feeling of bowel movement right after. Let me know if it works 🥰

Here’s a study on PubMed that you can read to learn more: “The effect of acupuncture at the Taiyang acupoint on visual function and EEG microstates in myopia”

text:
Niszczysz swoje trawienie 5 razy dziennie i nie masz pojęcia

Przez ostatnie tygodnie zagłębiałem się w fascynujący temat: czy tradycyjna medycyna chińska, która powstała tysiące lat przed wynalezieniem mikroskopu, mogła opisywać te same zjawiska fizjologiczne, które dziś badamy w laboratoriach? Odpowiedź jest zaskakująca.

Weźmy pięć klasycznych błędów żywieniowych według TCM. Jedzenie w pośpiechu, według chińskiej filozofii, "blokuje Chi" i osłabia trawienie. Brzmi ezoteryczne? Może. Ale gdy spojrzymy na badania z neurobiologii, okazuje się, że napięcie aktywuje układ współczulny, który dosłownie hamuje perystaltykę, zmniejsza wydzielanie enzymów i ogranicza przepływ krwi do przewodu pokarmowego. Badanie Kokkinosa i zespołu wykazało, że szybkie jedzenie obniża wydzielanie hormonów sytości GLP-1 i PYY o 25-30% (PMID: 19875483).

Kolejny przykład: TCM od wieków ostrzega przed piciem zimnej wody podczas posiłków, mówiąc, że "zabija ogień trawienia". Współczesne badania enzymatyczne pokazują, że obniżenie temperatury żołądka zmniejsza aktywność pepsyny i spowalnia opróżnianie żołądkowe.

Najbardziej uderzające jest to, co TCM nazywa "Chińskim Zegarem Biologicznym" - koncepcją, że każdy narząd ma swój szczyt aktywności o określonej porze dnia. Garaulet i zespół udowodnili, że późne jedzenie głównego posiłku (po 15:00) prowadzi do gorszych wyników redukcji masy ciała przy identycznej kaloryczności diety (PMID: 23357955). Scheer wykazał, że desynchronizacja rytmów dobowych zwiększa glukozę o 6%, insulinę o 22% i obniża leptynę o 17% (PMID: 19255424). TCM opisywała to 2000 lat wcześniej, używając innego języka.

Rozproszenie podczas jedzenia? Robinson przeprowadził metaanalizę 24 badań i odkrył, że jedzenie ze smartfonem zwiększa spożycie o 25% w późniejszych posiłkach przez zaburzoną pamięć epizodyczną posiłku (PMID: 23446890). TCM mówiła, że "obecność umysłu jest odżywianiem", nauka nazywa to fazą cefaliczną trawienia i interocepcją.

Co z tego wynika praktycznie? Pięć prostych zasad: jedz świadomie bez ekranów, pij ciepłe napoje z posiłkami, najwięcej jedz rano, jedz tylko gdy czujesz głód, ostatni posiłek przed zmrokiem.

Having a sore throat is one of the worst feelings everrrr🥹 if you know you know... I’m Chee Hee, a Chinese Medicine student from Malaysia 🇲🇾 and I’m graduating this year! Join me and follow along for more.

In this episode, I introduced an acupuncture point that is commonly used together to treat sore throat(LU11 ShaoShang). Acupressure treatment doesn’t directly combat the infection but helps alleviate the symptoms.

For sore throat relief, acupressure focuses on critical points in the body, one in particular. Stimulating this points can help alleviate throat pain and associated symptoms.

✨LU11, also known as Shaoshang, lies on the inner side of the thumb (ie opposite side of the thumb from the first finger) just proximal to the medial border of the nail where it meets the base of the nail.

Match the point on both hands and massage them against each other like you’re starting a small fire. Do this for 1-3 minutes. You should have a deep aching feeling on the point and a feeling of relief right after. ❄️ COLD-COLD SYMPTOMS:
Stiff neck
Stuffy + runny nose with clear, thin mucous
CHILLS, feel super cold, can’t get warm
Low or no fever
Desire to be under blankets
You recently stayed out in the cold too long

🔥 HOT-COLD SYMPTOMS
Really sore throat
Extremely thirsty
Fever, no chills
Cold sores
Feel hot and sweaty
Mild urge to cough with dry throat + tickle in the chest
Stuffy nose with yellow, sticky mucous
Red face, eyes

Many colds in winter start as Cold-Colds and can morph into Hot-Colds, especially if you’re dehydrated. Stay ahead of it by hydrating properly with warm beverages (think soups, teas, warm water).

Once you’re sick, your #1 job is to SLEEP (naps!) and HYDRATE like it’s your job. 🛌

Hot compress or Lanshin Hot Massager along the neck.
Fresh Ginger tea (make it spicy!)

It may not reinvent the franchise, but it gives context to the madness in a way that’s satisfying for longtime fans. If you’re into gritty horror, this one’s worth the watch.

[Recipe] In Traditional Chinese Medicine, sweet fermented rice wine is a “warming” food that boosts Qi (energy), invigorates blood circulation, aids digestion by providing probiotics, strengthens the immune system, and offers warmth, making it great for recovery and can also ease menstrual cramps by improving blood flow.

Sweet fermented rice with orange tea is a warm drink made by heating sweet fermented rice (laozao / Jiu Niang) with fresh orange slices or/and orange juice. It combines the sweet and soft texture of fermented rice with the refreshing aroma of oranges, making it very nourishing, especially suitable for autumn and winter as it warms the body and aids digestion.

The preparation method of this drink is simple and you can add other ingredients such as red dates and goji berries, to further elevate the nutritional values and flavour of this comforting dessert.

Ingredients 
1 large Navel Orange (remove the skin)
4 seedless red dates
1 tsp of goji berries

Warm tea, warm breakfasts, warm gut. It changed everything.

W Chinach o 13:00 biurowce cichną jak po odcięciu prądu, spotkania kończą się automatycznie, a ludzie kładą głowy na biurkach. To wuxiu - południowa drzemka, prawo zakorzenione w kulturze tak głęboko, jak u nas poranna kawa. Dla Chińczyków to część higieny energetycznej.

Według zegara organów TCM, między 13:00 a 15:00 szczyt aktywności ma meridian jelita cienkiego, czyli ten, który „oddziela czyste od nieczystego”, zarówno w trawieniu, jak i w emocjach. Brzmi metaforycznie? To posłuchaj współczesnej nauki.
Chronobiologia mówi dokładnie to samo, tylko innymi słowami: post-prandial dip, naturalny spadek czujności po posiłku. O Tribunal de Contas dos Municípios da Bahia (TCM) aprovou, nesta terça-feira (9), as contas do exercício de 2024 do ex-prefeito de Camaçari, Elinaldo Araújo (@elinaldooficial) (União Brasil). 

Com isso, o ex-gestor conclui seus dois mandatos consecutivos com todas as contas anuais validadas pela Corte, fato considerado raro entre grandes municípios da Bahia.

O parecer, relatado pela conselheira Aline Peixoto, confirmou o cumprimento integral das obrigações fiscais, incluindo investimentos mínimos em educação e saúde, além do respeito aos limites da Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal. 

Somente em 2024, o orçamento administrado por Elinaldo chegou a R$ 2,3 bilhões.

Elinaldo comemorou o resultado e afirmou que o parecer consolida o modelo de gestão implantado ao longo de oito anos.

“Encerrar dois mandatos com 100% das contas aprovadas mostra que fizemos uma administração responsável, técnica e transparente. Mantivemos equilíbrio fiscal, investimos nas áreas essenciais e entregamos uma prefeitura organizada”, disse.

O ex-gestor também ressaltou o papel da equipe.
“Esse resultado não pertence a uma pessoa, mas a toda a estrutura administrativa. Cada secretaria contribuiu para que Camaçari pudesse cumprir a legislação, manter as finanças em ordem e continuar avançando”, afirmou.

Além da validação do TCM, Elinaldo destacou indicadores nacionais que reforçam a evolução fiscal e administrativa do município. Ele lembrou que Camaçari elevou sua Capacidade de Pagamento (Capag) junto ao Tesouro Nacional e apresentou crescimento no Índice Firjan de Desenvolvimento Municipal (IFDM).

Segundo dados mencionados pelo ex-prefeito, o município subiu de 0,5100 para 0,6380, saindo de baixo para moderado desenvolvimento no período analisado.

Heilsame Körperpunkte - Lunge 1 hilft bei Husten und Bronchitis

Am einfachsten findest du Lunge 1, wenn du die Hand in die Achselhöhle legst und dort, wo der gestreckte Daumen am Brustkorb landet, ist der Punkt, circa zwei Fingerbreiten unterhalb des Schlüsselbeins, in einer Vertiefung am Brustmuskel. Mach eine lockere Faust und klopfe den Bereich ganz sanft ab

Lunge 1, die „Zentrale Residenz“ stärkt und beruhigt das Atemsystem,  hilft bei Husten & Bronchitis und ist ein wichtiger Punkt bei Asthma. Er fördert grundsätzlich die Abwehrkräfte des Körpers und hat die stärkste Wirkung auf das Organ Lunge selbst.

Die Lunge spielt in der TCM eine wichtige Rolle bei der Versorgung des Körpers mit Qi, der kosmischen Lebensenergie aus der Atemluft, die auch wichtig für unsere Abwehrkräfte und damit für das Immunsystem ist. Lunge 1 hilft, Schleim umzuwandeln, und reguliert die Wasserzirkulation.

Da auch jede Pore unserer Haut atmet, ist sie aus chinesischer Sicht ein Teil der Lungen. Die Haut ist die natürliche Grenze unseres Selbst. Es geht um den Austausch mit der Außenwelt und um eine gesunde Abgrenzung zu dieser.

Wenn dieser Punkt schmerzhaft ist, ist es besonders wichtig, sich um die Atmung zu kümmern. Du kannst den Punkt 2-3 Mal am Tag auf beiden Seiten sanft ausklopfen oder massieren.
